**Container Orchestration Details:**

**ECS Task Management:**
- **Task Definition**: Specifies container images, resource requirements (CPU/memory), environment variables
- **Service Definition**: Defines desired task count, load balancing, and deployment configuration
- **Task Placement**: Spread tasks across availability zones for high availability
- **Resource Reservation**: CPU units and memory allocated per container

**Auto Scaling Configuration:**

**Target Tracking Policies:**
1. **CPU Utilization Target**: 70% average CPU utilization
   - Scale up when average > 70% for 2 minutes
   - Scale down when average < 50% for 10 minutes
2. **Request Count Target**: 1000 requests per task per minute
3. **Custom Metrics**: Application-specific metrics (e.g., queue length, AI processing jobs)

**Scaling Limits:**
- **Minimum Tasks**: 2 (high availability)
- **Maximum Tasks**: 20 (cost control)
- **Scaling Cooldown**: 5-minute cooldown between scaling activities
- **Scale-Up Speed**: Aggressive (add multiple tasks quickly)
- **Scale-Down Speed**: Conservative (gradual task termination)

**Connection Draining:**
- **Draining Timeout**: 300 seconds (5 minutes)
- **New Request Handling**: Drained tasks reject new requests
- **In-Flight Requests**: Allowed to complete within timeout period
- **Graceful Shutdown**: SIGTERM signal sent to containers for cleanup

**Health Check Configuration:**
- **Health Check Path**: `/health`
- **Health Check Interval**: 30 seconds
- **Healthy Threshold**: 2 consecutive successful checks
- **Unhealthy Threshold**: 3 consecutive failed checks
- **Timeout**: 5 seconds per health check

**Cost Optimization:**
- **Spot Instances**: Use EC2 Spot Instances for non-critical tasks (up to 70% cost savings)
- **Right-Sizing**: Regular analysis of resource utilization for optimal task sizing
- **Scheduled Scaling**: Predictable load patterns utilize scheduled scaling policies
- **Idle Resource Detection**: Automated alerts for underutilized resources

## 4.5 State Management and Transaction Flows [PLANNED]

### 4.5.1 Application State Lifecycle

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Uninitialized
    
    Uninitialized --> Initializing: Application Start
    Initializing --> Loading: Load Configuration
    Loading --> Authenticating: Connect to Services
    Authenticating --> Ready: Authentication Success
    Authenticating --> Error: Authentication Failure
    
    Ready --> Processing: Receive Request
    Processing --> CacheCheck: Check Cache
    CacheCheck --> CacheHit: Data Found
    CacheCheck --> CacheMiss: Data Not Found
    
    CacheHit --> ResponseReady: Return Cached Data
    CacheMiss --> DatabaseQuery: Query Database
    DatabaseQuery --> DataValidation: Validate Data
    DataValidation --> AIProcessing: AI Required
    DataValidation --> ResponseReady: No AI Required
    
    AIProcessing --> AISuccess: Processing Complete
    AIProcessing --> AIError: Processing Failed
    AISuccess --> ResponseReady: Format Response
    AIError --> Retry: Retry Available
    AIError --> FallbackState: No Retry
    
    Retry --> AIProcessing: Retry Attempt
    FallbackState --> ResponseReady: Use Fallback Data
    
    ResponseReady --> CacheUpdate: Update Cache
    CacheUpdate --> Ready: Response Sent
    
    Processing --> Error: Unhandled Exception
    DatabaseQuery --> Error: Database Unavailable
    
    Error --> Recovery: Attempt Recovery
    Recovery --> Ready: Recovery Success
    Recovery --> Degraded: Partial Recovery
    Recovery --> Failed: Recovery Failed
    
    Degraded --> Ready: Services Restored
    Degraded --> Maintenance: Manual Intervention
    
    Maintenance --> Ready: Maintenance Complete
    
    Ready --> Shutting Down: Shutdown Signal
    Processing --> Shutting Down: Graceful Shutdown
    Shutting Down --> Draining: Drain Connections
    Draining --> Cleanup: Cleanup Resources
    Cleanup --> [*]: Shutdown Complete
    
    Failed --> [*]: Critical Failure
```

**State Management Components:**

**Application Initialization States:**
1. **Uninitialized**: Container started, no services loaded
2. **Initializing**: Loading application configuration, environment variables
3. **Loading**: Establishing database connections, cache connections
4. **Authenticating**: Validating AWS credentials, Auth0 configuration
5. **Ready**: Healthy state, accepting incoming requests

**Request Processing States:**
- **Processing**: Active request handling in progress
- **CacheCheck**: Querying Redis cache for existing data
- **DatabaseQuery**: Executing MongoDB queries
- **AIProcessing**: LangChain pipeline execution with OpenAI
- **ResponseReady**: Formatted response ready for transmission

**Error and Recovery States:**
- **Error**: Unhandled exception or service failure detected
- **Recovery**: Attempting automatic recovery procedures
- **Degraded**: Operating with reduced functionality
- **Maintenance**: Manual intervention required
- **Failed**: Unrecoverable failure, container termination required

**Shutdown States:**
- **Shutting Down**: Graceful shutdown initiated (SIGTERM received)
- **Draining**: Rejecting new requests, completing in-flight requests
- **Cleanup**: Closing database connections, flushing logs
- **Shutdown Complete**: Container exits with status code

### 4.5.2 Database Transaction Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Flask Application
    participant Session as MongoDB Session
    participant DB as MongoDB
    participant Cache as Redis Cache
    participant CloudWatch as CloudWatch Logs
    
    App->>Session: Start Transaction
    Session->>DB: Begin Transaction
    DB-->>Session: Transaction ID
    
    App->>Session: Execute Operation 1 (Insert User)
    Session->>DB: Insert Document
    DB-->>Session: WriteResult (Pending)
    
    App->>Session: Execute Operation 2 (Update Profile)
    Session->>DB: Update Document
    DB-->>Session: WriteResult (Pending)
    
    App->>Session: Execute Operation 3 (Insert Audit Log)
    Session->>DB: Insert Document
    DB-->>Session: WriteResult (Pending)
    
    alt All Operations Successful
        App->>Session: Commit Transaction
        Session->>DB: Commit
        DB->>DB: Apply All Changes Atomically
        DB-->>Session: Commit Success
        Session-->>App: Transaction Complete
        
        App->>Cache: Invalidate Related Cache Keys
        Cache-->>App: Keys Invalidated
        
        App->>CloudWatch: Log Transaction Success
    else Any Operation Failed
        App->>Session: Abort Transaction
        Session->>DB: Rollback
        DB->>DB: Discard All Pending Changes
        DB-->>Session: Rollback Complete
        Session-->>App: Transaction Aborted
        
        App->>CloudWatch: Log Transaction Failure
        
        App->>App: Determine Retry Strategy
        
        alt Retryable Error (Network Issue)
            App->>Session: Start New Transaction
        else Non-Retryable Error (Validation)
            App->>App: Return Error to Client
        end
    end
```

**Transaction Management Principles:**

**ACID Properties:**
1. **Atomicity**: All operations within transaction succeed or all fail
2. **Consistency**: Database remains in valid state before and after transaction
3. **Isolation**: Concurrent transactions do not interfere (snapshot isolation)
4. **Durability**: Committed transactions persist through system failures

**MongoDB Transaction Configuration:**
- **Write Concern**: `w: "majority"` - Write acknowledged by majority of replica set members
- **Read Concern**: `readConcern: "snapshot"` - Consistent snapshot isolation
- **Transaction Timeout**: 60 seconds maximum duration
- **Retry Logic**: Transient transaction errors (network issues) automatically retried

**Transaction Boundaries:**
- **User Registration**: User document + profile document + audit log (single transaction)
- **Payment Processing**: Order creation + inventory update + payment record (single transaction)
- **Batch Operations**: Chunked into multiple transactions (e.g., 100 documents per transaction)

**Cache Coherency:**
- **Pessimistic Invalidation**: Cache invalidated before transaction commit
- **Optimistic Invalidation**: Cache invalidated after successful transaction
- **Selective Invalidation**: Only affected cache keys invalidated (not blanket cache clear)

**Error Handling:**
- **TransientTransactionError**: Automatically retried (network issues, temporary locks)
- **DuplicateKeyError**: Not retried (constraint violation)
- **ValidationError**: Not retried (schema validation failure)
- **TimeoutError**: Retried with exponential backoff

## 4.6 Integration Workflow Patterns [PLANNED]

### 4.6.1 Third-Party Service Integration Sequence

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client as Client Application
    participant ALB as AWS ALB
    participant Flask as Flask Backend
    participant Auth0
    participant OpenAI
    participant MongoDB
    participant Redis as Redis Cache
    participant CloudWatch
    
    Client->>ALB: API Request
    ALB->>Flask: Route Request
    
    Flask->>Redis: Check Circuit Breaker State
    Redis-->>Flask: Circuit Closed
    
    Flask->>Auth0: Validate JWT Token
    
    alt Token Valid
        Auth0-->>Flask: Token Claims
    else Token Invalid
        Auth0-->>Flask: 401 Unauthorized
        Flask->>Client: Return 401
    end
    
    Flask->>Redis: Check Response Cache
    
    alt Cache Hit
        Redis-->>Flask: Cached Response
        Flask->>Client: Return Cached Data
    else Cache Miss
        Flask->>MongoDB: Query User Context
        MongoDB-->>Flask: User Data
        
        Flask->>OpenAI: Generate AI Response
        
        alt OpenAI Success
            OpenAI-->>Flask: AI Response
            Flask->>MongoDB: Store Interaction
            MongoDB-->>Flask: Stored
            
            Flask->>Redis: Cache Response (TTL: 300s)
            Redis-->>Flask: Cached
            
            Flask->>Client: Return AI Response
        else OpenAI Timeout
            Flask->>Redis: Record Failure
            Redis->>Redis: Increment Failure Count
            
            alt Failure Threshold Exceeded
                Redis->>Redis: Open Circuit Breaker
                Flask->>Client: Return Cached/Default Response
            else Retry Available
                Flask->>OpenAI: Retry with Backoff
            end
        else OpenAI Rate Limit
            Flask->>Redis: Check Rate Limit State
            Flask->>Client: Return 429 Too Many Requests
        end
    end
    
    Flask->>CloudWatch: Log Request Metrics
```

**Integration Patterns:**

**1. Auth0 Authentication Integration:**
- **Protocol**: OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect
- **Token Validation**: JWT signature verification using Auth0 public keys (JWKS endpoint)
- **Token Refresh**: Automatic refresh using refresh tokens before expiration
- **Fallback**: Cached user permissions used if Auth0 temporarily unavailable

**2. OpenAI API Integration:**
- **Rate Limiting**: Respect OpenAI rate limits (requests per minute, tokens per minute)
- **Request Queuing**: Queue requests when approaching rate limits
- **Streaming**: Server-Sent Events (SSE) for streaming responses
- **Cost Management**: Token usage tracking and per-user budget enforcement
- **Model Selection**: Automatic fallback from GPT-4 to GPT-3.5 based on availability and cost

**3. MongoDB Atlas Integration:**
- **Connection Pooling**: Maintain connection pool (min: 10, max: 100 connections)
- **Read Preference**: Primary for writes, secondary for read-heavy operations
- **Retry Writes**: Automatic retry for transient write failures
- **Change Streams**: Real-time change notification for reactive features

**4. AWS Service Integration:**
- **S3**: Pre-signed URLs for secure file uploads/downloads
- **CloudWatch**: Structured logging with context propagation
- **ECR**: Automated image pulls with IAM role authentication
- **Parameter Store**: Secure configuration and secrets management

**Event-Driven Architecture (Planned for Future Implementation):**

**Event Types:**
1. **Domain Events**:
   - `user.registered`: New user account created
   - `ai.request.completed`: AI processing finished
   - `data.updated`: Database record modified
   - `error.critical`: Critical system error occurred

2. **Integration Events**:

   - `payment.received`: Payment processing completed

3. **System Events**:

   - `scaling.triggered`: Auto-scaling event occurred

```json
  }
}
```

**Event Processing Guarantees:**
- **At-Least-Once Delivery**: Events delivered at least once (may have duplicates)
- **Idempotency**: Event handlers designed to handle duplicate events safely
- **Ordering**: FIFO queues for order-sensitive events
- **Dead Letter Queues**: Failed events routed to DLQ for manual investigation

## 4.7 Validation Rules and Checkpoints [PLANNED]

### 4.7.1 Request Validation Pipeline

```mermaid
graph TB
    IncomingRequest((Incoming Request))
    
    subgraph "Pre-Processing Validation"
        ContentType{Valid Content-Type?}
        ContentLength{Content-Length<br/>Within Limits?}
        RateLimit{Rate Limit<br/>Check?}
    end
    
    subgraph "Authentication Validation"
        TokenPresent{Token<br/>Present?}
        TokenFormat{Valid JWT<br/>Format?}
        TokenSignature{Valid<br/>Signature?}
        TokenExpiry{Token<br/>Expired?}
    end
    
    subgraph "Schema Validation"
        ParseJSON{Valid<br/>JSON?}
        ValidateSchema{Schema<br/>Valid?}
        RequiredFields{All Required<br/>Fields Present?}
        FieldTypes{Field Types<br/>Correct?}
        FieldConstraints{Constraints<br/>Satisfied?}
    end
    
    subgraph "Business Rule Validation"
        CheckPermissions{User Has<br/>Permissions?}
        ResourceExists{Resource<br/>Exists?}
        StateValid{Valid State<br/>Transition?}
        BusinessRules{Business Rules<br/>Satisfied?}
    end
    
    subgraph "Security Validation"
        SQLInjection{SQL Injection<br/>Check?}
        XSSCheck{XSS Attack<br/>Check?}
        CSRFToken{CSRF Token<br/>Valid?}
        IPWhitelist{IP<br/>Whitelisted?}
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing"
        ProcessRequest[Process Valid Request]
        Success((Return Success))
    end
    
    subgraph "Error Responses"
        Error400[400 Bad Request]
        Error401[401 Unauthorized]
        Error403[403 Forbidden]
        Error404[404 Not Found]
        Error413[413 Payload Too Large]
        Error422[422 Unprocessable Entity]
        Error429[429 Too Many Requests]
    end
    
    IncomingRequest --> ContentType
    ContentType -->|Invalid| Error400
    ContentType -->|Valid| ContentLength
    
    ContentLength -->|Too Large| Error413
    ContentLength -->|Valid| RateLimit
    
    RateLimit -->|Exceeded| Error429
    RateLimit -->|OK| TokenPresent
    
    TokenPresent -->|No| Error401
    TokenPresent -->|Yes| TokenFormat
    
    TokenFormat -->|Invalid| Error401
    TokenFormat -->|Valid| TokenSignature
    
    TokenSignature -->|Invalid| Error401
    TokenSignature -->|Valid| TokenExpiry
    
    TokenExpiry -->|Expired| Error401
    TokenExpiry -->|Valid| ParseJSON
    
    ParseJSON -->|Invalid| Error400
    ParseJSON -->|Valid| ValidateSchema
    
    ValidateSchema -->|Invalid| Error422
    ValidateSchema -->|Valid| RequiredFields
    
    RequiredFields -->|Missing| Error422
    RequiredFields -->|Present| FieldTypes
    
    FieldTypes -->|Invalid| Error422
    FieldTypes -->|Valid| FieldConstraints
    
    FieldConstraints -->|Violated| Error422
    FieldConstraints -->|Satisfied| CheckPermissions
    
    CheckPermissions -->|Denied| Error403
    CheckPermissions -->|Granted| ResourceExists
    
    ResourceExists -->|Not Found| Error404
    ResourceExists -->|Exists| StateValid
    
    StateValid -->|Invalid| Error422
    StateValid -->|Valid| BusinessRules
    
    BusinessRules -->|Violated| Error422
    BusinessRules -->|Satisfied| SQLInjection
    
    SQLInjection -->|Detected| Error400
    SQLInjection -->|Clean| XSSCheck
    
    XSSCheck -->|Detected| Error400
    XSSCheck -->|Clean| CSRFToken
    
    CSRFToken -->|Invalid| Error403
    CSRFToken -->|Valid| IPWhitelist
    
    IPWhitelist -->|Not Whitelisted| Error403
    IPWhitelist -->|Whitelisted| ProcessRequest
    
    ProcessRequest --> Success
```

**Validation Checkpoints:**

**1. Pre-Processing Validation:**
- **Content-Type**: Verify `application/json` for API requests
- **Content-Length**: Enforce maximum payload size (default: 10MB)
- **Rate Limiting**: Per-user and per-IP rate limits enforced
- **CORS**: Cross-origin request validation for web clients

**2. Authentication Validation:**
- **Token Presence**: JWT token required in Authorization header
- **Token Format**: Valid JWT structure (header.payload.signature)
- **Signature Verification**: Validate signature using Auth0 public key
- **Expiration Check**: Reject expired tokens with grace period (30 seconds)
- **Claims Validation**: Required claims (`sub`, `exp`, `iat`, `aud`) present and valid

**3. Schema Validation:**
- **JSON Parsing**: Validate well-formed JSON structure
- **Schema Definition**: Pydantic models or JSON Schema validators
- **Required Fields**: All mandatory fields present with non-null values
- **Type Checking**: Field types match schema (string, int, bool, array, object)
- **Constraints**: Range validation, string length, regex patterns, enum values

**4. Business Rule Validation:**
- **Permission Checks**: User roles and permissions verified against resource requirements
- **Resource Existence**: Referenced resources (user IDs, document IDs) exist in database
- **State Transitions**: Valid state machine transitions (e.g., draft → published, but not published → draft)
- **Domain Rules**: Business-specific validation (e.g., minimum age, valid postal code)

**5. Security Validation:**
- **SQL Injection Prevention**: Input sanitization (though MongoDB reduces risk)
- **XSS Prevention**: HTML entity encoding for user-generated content
- **CSRF Protection**: Validate CSRF tokens for state-changing operations
- **IP Whitelisting**: Optional IP-based access control for sensitive operations

**Validation Error Response Format:**
```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "VALIDATION_ERROR",
    "message": "Request validation failed",
    "details": [
      {
        "field": "email",
        "error": "Invalid email format",
        "constraint": "Must be a valid email address"
      },
      {
        "field": "age",
        "error": "Value out of range",
        "constraint": "Must be between 18 and 120"
      }
    ],
    "request_id": "req-uuid-1234"
  }
}
```

### 4.7.2 Data Validation and Sanitization

**Input Sanitization Rules:**

1. **String Fields:**
   - Trim leading/trailing whitespace
   - Remove control characters
   - Validate against maximum length
   - Optional regex pattern matching

2. **Numeric Fields:**
   - Parse to appropriate type (int, float)
   - Validate min/max ranges
   - Check for NaN and Infinity values

3. **Date/Time Fields:**
   - ISO 8601 format validation
   - Timezone handling (convert to UTC)
   - Historical date validation (prevent future dates where inappropriate)

4. **Array Fields:**
   - Validate minimum/maximum length
   - Validate each element against schema
   - Check for duplicate elements (if required)

5. **Object Fields:**
   - Recursive schema validation
   - Check for required nested fields
   - Validate nested field types

**Output Sanitization:**
- **PII Masking**: Sensitive data (SSN, credit cards) partially masked in logs
- **HTML Encoding**: User-generated content HTML-encoded before display
- **JSON Escaping**: Special characters escaped in JSON responses
- **SQL Escaping**: Query parameters properly escaped (parameterized queries)

**Performance Optimization Strategies:**

- **Query Optimization**: MongoDB indexes on frequently queried fields
- **Connection Pooling**: Reuse database and HTTP connections
- **Async Processing**: Non-critical operations processed asynchronously

# 5. System Architecture

## 5.1 High-Level Architecture

### 5.1.1 System Overview

#### 5.1.1.1 Architectural Style and Rationale

The NewNov_6_1 system is designed as a **multi-tier, cloud-native, microservices-ready architecture** that prioritizes scalability, maintainability, and platform ubiquity. This architectural approach has been selected to support ambitious multi-platform requirements spanning web, mobile (cross-platform and native), and desktop (cross-platform and native) applications, all powered by a unified backend infrastructure.

**Architectural Pattern:** The system implements a **three-tier architecture** enhanced with dedicated caching and content delivery layers:

1. **Presentation Layer:** Multi-platform frontend applications (React web, React Native mobile, native iOS/Android/macOS apps, Electron desktop)
2. **Application Layer:** Stateless Python Flask backend services with AI orchestration capabilities via LangChain
3. **Data Layer:** Document-based persistence (MongoDB), distributed caching (Redis), and object storage (AWS S3)
4. **Edge Layer:** Global content delivery network (AWS CloudFront) for performance optimization

This layered approach provides clear separation of concerns while enabling each tier to scale independently based on demand patterns.

#### 5.1.1.2 Core Architectural Principles

The technology selections and architectural decisions adhere to five foundational principles that guide all implementation choices:

**Industry Standard Adoption:** The architecture leverages battle-tested technologies with extensive community support and proven production track records. Python, React, MongoDB, and AWS represent industry-dominant choices that ensure long-term viability, extensive documentation, and availability of engineering talent.

**Cloud-Native Design:** Built from inception for cloud deployment, the architecture embraces containerization (Docker), infrastructure-as-code (Terraform), managed services (MongoDB Atlas, AWS ElastiCache), and elastic scaling patterns. This cloud-native approach eliminates infrastructure management overhead while providing enterprise-grade reliability and global reach.

**Polyglot Platform Strategy:** Rather than forcing a single technology across all platforms, the architecture optimizes language selection per platform requirements. Backend services use Python for productivity and AI integration, web applications leverage TypeScript for type safety, and native mobile/desktop applications employ platform-native languages (Swift, Kotlin, Objective-C) where performance and platform integration justify the investment.

**Modern Development Practices:** The architecture incorporates contemporary DevOps methodologies including continuous integration/continuous deployment (GitHub Actions), containerized deployment (ECS), infrastructure versioning (Terraform), and comprehensive monitoring (CloudWatch). These practices accelerate development velocity while maintaining production stability.

**AI-Ready Infrastructure:** Recognizing artificial intelligence as a core system capability rather than an afterthought, the architecture integrates LangChain framework at the application layer, supports vector databases for semantic search, and provides flexible LLM provider integration (OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock). This AI-first design enables intelligent features throughout the application.

#### 5.1.1.3 System Boundaries and Major Interfaces

The system defines clear boundaries between internal components and external integrations:

**Internal System Boundary:** Encompasses all application code, containerized services, databases, caches, and AWS infrastructure provisioned via Terraform. These components operate within a controlled Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) with network isolation and security group protection.

**External Integration Boundary:** Interfaces with managed third-party services including Auth0 for authentication, LLM providers for AI capabilities, and vector databases for semantic search. These integrations occur over encrypted HTTPS connections with API key authentication.

**User Boundary:** Multiple client applications across web browsers, mobile devices, and desktop platforms communicate exclusively through the Application Load Balancer (ALB), which serves as the single ingress point for all API traffic. Static assets are delivered via CloudFront CDN, completely bypassing backend infrastructure.

**Administrative Boundary:** Infrastructure management occurs through Terraform configurations, GitHub Actions workflows, and AWS console access, all protected by multi-factor authentication and least-privilege IAM policies.

### 5.1.2 Core Components

The following table catalogs the major architectural components, their responsibilities, dependencies, and integration characteristics:

| Component Name | Primary Responsibility | Key Dependencies | Integration Points |
|----------------|----------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Application Load Balancer** | Traffic distribution, SSL termination, health checking | AWS VPC, Target Groups, SSL certificates | All client applications, Flask backend instances |
| **Flask API Services** | RESTful endpoints, business logic, request orchestration | Python runtime, Flask extensions, PyMongo, redis-py, boto3 | ALB, MongoDB, Redis, S3, Auth0, LangChain |
| **LangChain Orchestration** | AI workflow management, LLM integration, prompt engineering | OpenAI/Anthropic SDKs, Vector DB clients | Flask services, LLM providers, Vector databases |
| **MongoDB Atlas** | Primary data persistence, document storage, vector search | Network connectivity, IAM authentication | Flask services via PyMongo driver |

| Component Name | Primary Responsibility | Key Dependencies | Integration Points |
|----------------|----------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Redis Cache** | Response caching, session storage, rate limiting | ElastiCache cluster | Flask services via redis-py, Celery job queue |
| **AWS S3** | Object storage, file uploads, backups, static assets | IAM roles, bucket policies | Flask services via boto3, CloudFront CDN |
| **CloudFront CDN** | Global content delivery, edge caching, static hosting | S3 origin, SSL certificates | S3 buckets, client applications |
| **Auth0 Platform** | Authentication, JWT issuance, user management, MFA | OAuth 2.0 configuration | All client applications, Flask JWT validation middleware |

| Component Name | Primary Responsibility | Key Dependencies | Integration Points |
|----------------|----------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **ECS Cluster** | Container orchestration, deployment, auto-scaling | Docker images, task definitions, service definitions | ECR container registry, ALB target groups, CloudWatch |
| **React Web Application** | Browser-based user interface | Node.js, React 18+, TypeScript, TailwindCSS | ALB API endpoints, Auth0, CloudFront static hosting |
| **React Native Mobile** | Cross-platform iOS/Android mobile app | React Native runtime, platform SDKs | ALB API endpoints, Auth0 |
| **Native Applications** | Platform-specific iOS/Android/macOS experiences | Swift/Kotlin/Objective-C, platform frameworks | ALB API endpoints, Auth0 |

**Critical Architectural Considerations:**

- **Stateless Backend Design:** Flask services maintain no session state, enabling horizontal scaling through simple instance replication behind the load balancer
- **Distributed Caching:** Redis provides shared state across multiple backend instances for session data and rate limiting
- **Database Connection Pooling:** PyMongo connection pools prevent database connection exhaustion during traffic spikes
- **Asynchronous Processing:** Celery with Redis broker enables background job processing for long-running operations
- **Direct S3 Upload:** Pre-signed URLs allow clients to upload files directly to S3, bypassing backend infrastructure and reducing server load
- **JWT-Based Authentication:** Stateless token validation eliminates backend authentication state and session storage requirements

### 5.1.3 Data Flow Architecture

#### 5.1.3.1 Primary Request Flow Patterns

**Standard API Request Flow:**

The typical user-initiated API request follows a multi-layer validation and processing path. A client application (web, mobile, or desktop) initiates an HTTPS request that first reaches the AWS Application Load Balancer. The ALB performs SSL termination, health-based routing, and distributes the request to an available Flask backend instance within the ECS cluster.

Upon receiving the request, Flask middleware validates the JWT token by verifying its signature and expiration against Auth0 public keys. Once authenticated, the backend checks the Redis cache for a matching cached response using a cache key derived from the request path and parameters. If a valid cached response exists (cache hit), the backend immediately returns the cached data, avoiding database queries entirely.

On cache miss, the Flask service queries MongoDB using PyMongo, applying appropriate filters and projections. The database returns BSON documents, which Flask transforms into JSON responses. Before returning to the client, cacheable responses are stored in Redis with appropriate time-to-live (TTL) values. The JSON response flows back through the ALB to the client application, where it updates the user interface.

Throughout this flow, CloudWatch captures metrics (request count, latency, error rates) and logs (request details, errors, warnings) for monitoring and troubleshooting.

**AI-Enhanced Request Flow:**

Requests requiring artificial intelligence processing follow an extended path through the LangChain orchestration layer. After standard authentication and authorization, Flask routes AI-specific requests to the LangChain integration module. LangChain retrieves relevant context from the vector database using semantic similarity search on stored embeddings. This retrieved context, combined with the user's request, forms a structured prompt sent to the configured LLM provider (OpenAI GPT-4, Anthropic Claude, or AWS Bedrock).

The LLM processes the prompt and returns a generated response. LangChain post-processes this response, potentially performing additional validation, formatting, or follow-up requests. Flask stores the complete conversation exchange (user input, context used, LLM response) in MongoDB for future reference and system improvement. The formatted AI response returns to the client through the standard response path.

**File Upload Flow:**

File uploads utilize a direct-to-S3 pattern that minimizes backend involvement. The client requests a pre-signed S3 URL from the Flask API, providing the intended filename, content type, and target storage location. Flask generates a temporary, cryptographically signed URL using boto3 and the S3 PutObject operation, with a short expiration window (typically 5-15 minutes).

The client receives this pre-signed URL and performs a direct HTTPS PUT request to S3, completely bypassing backend infrastructure. This approach significantly reduces backend load, improves upload performance, and leverages S3's superior bandwidth and reliability. Upon successful upload, the client notifies the Flask API, which stores file metadata (key, size, content type, upload timestamp) in MongoDB for future reference. If the file should be publicly accessible, CloudFront provides cached, globally distributed access.

**Authentication Flow:**

User authentication leverages Auth0's managed authentication platform. When a user initiates login, the client redirects to Auth0's hosted authentication page. Auth0 handles credential validation, multi-factor authentication (if enabled), social provider integration, and security monitoring. Upon successful authentication, Auth0 returns a JWT access token and refresh token to the client via redirect callback.

The client stores these tokens securely (httpOnly cookies for web, secure storage for mobile) and includes the access token in the Authorization header for all subsequent API requests. Flask backend services validate tokens on every request by verifying the JWT signature using Auth0's public keys, checking expiration, and extracting user identity and permissions from token claims. This stateless authentication approach scales horizontally without session storage.

#### 5.1.3.2 Data Transformation Points

**Client-to-Backend Transformation:** Frontend TypeScript interfaces and models serialize to JSON for transmission. Backend Flask services deserialize JSON into Python dictionaries or Pydantic models for validation and type safety.

**Backend-to-Database Transformation:** Python objects serialize to BSON (Binary JSON) format for MongoDB storage. PyMongo handles this transformation transparently, maintaining Python data types including datetime, ObjectId, and binary data.

**AI Integration Transformation:** User inputs and system data transform into structured prompts following LangChain template patterns. LLM responses (unstructured text) are parsed and structured into JSON responses for client consumption.

**Storage Transformation:** Files uploaded to S3 maintain their native binary format. Metadata extracted during upload (content type, size, checksums) stores as MongoDB documents linking to S3 object keys.

#### 5.1.3.3 Multi-Layer Caching Strategy

The architecture implements four caching layers, each optimized for different access patterns:

**Browser Cache:** Client applications cache static assets (JavaScript bundles, CSS stylesheets, images) using HTTP Cache-Control headers. Service workers (if implemented as Progressive Web App) provide offline-first experiences by caching API responses and assets locally.

**CDN Edge Cache:** CloudFront distributions cache static assets and potentially cacheable API responses at edge locations globally, reducing latency for geographically distributed users. Cache invalidation occurs through versioned asset paths (cache-busting) or explicit invalidation requests.

**Application Cache:** Redis stores frequently accessed API responses, user session data, rate limiting counters, and temporary data (OTP codes, verification tokens). This distributed cache spans all Flask instances, providing consistent data regardless of which instance handles a request.

**Database Query Cache:** MongoDB's WiredTiger storage engine maintains an internal cache of frequently accessed documents and indexes in memory, accelerating repeated queries without application-level caching logic.

### 5.1.4 External Integration Points

The system integrates with managed third-party services to leverage specialized capabilities without building and maintaining complex infrastructure:

| System Name | Integration Type | Data Exchange Pattern | Protocol/Format |
|-------------|-----------------|----------------------|-----------------|
| **Auth0** | Managed Authentication | OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, token validation | HTTPS, JWT tokens, OpenID Connect |
| **MongoDB Atlas** | Managed Database | Read/write operations, aggregations, vector search | MongoDB wire protocol over TLS, BSON |
| **AWS Services** | Cloud Infrastructure | Compute, storage, networking, monitoring API calls | AWS REST APIs, HTTPS, JSON/XML |
| **OpenAI** | LLM Provider | Prompt submission, streaming completion responses | HTTPS REST API, JSON, Server-Sent Events |

| System Name | Integration Type | Data Exchange Pattern | Protocol/Format |
|-------------|-----------------|----------------------|-----------------|
| **Anthropic Claude** | LLM Provider (Alternative) | Prompt submission, completion responses | HTTPS REST API, JSON |
| **Vector Database** | Semantic Search | Embedding storage, similarity queries | Service-specific API (Pinecone/Weaviate/Chroma) |
| **GitHub** | Source Control & CI/CD | Repository management, webhook triggers | Git protocol, GitHub Actions, HTTPS |
| **AWS ElastiCache** | Managed Redis | Cache operations, pub/sub messaging | Redis wire protocol over TLS |

**Service Level Agreement Requirements:**

- **Auth0:** 99.99% uptime SLA, sub-200ms authentication response times
- **MongoDB Atlas:** 99.95% uptime for M10+ clusters, automated backups with point-in-time recovery
- **AWS Core Services:** 99.9-99.99% uptime depending on service (EC2, S3, ECS), multi-AZ deployment recommended
- **LLM Providers:** Variable based on provider and plan; typically 99%+ uptime with rate limiting considerations
- **Vector Databases:** Varies by provider; Pinecone offers 99.9% SLA on paid plans

**Integration Security Posture:**

All external integrations require encrypted connections (TLS 1.3), API key or token-based authentication, and secrets stored in AWS Secrets Manager rather than code or configuration files. Network-level restrictions (security groups, IP allowlisting where supported) provide defense-in-depth. Rate limiting and circuit breakers protect against cascading failures from external service disruptions.

## 5.2 Component Details

### 5.2.1 Presentation Layer Components

#### 5.2.1.1 React Web Application

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

The React web application serves as the primary browser-based interface for desktop and mobile web users. Built with React 18+ leveraging concurrent rendering features, the application provides a responsive, accessible, and performant user experience across modern browsers. The component-based architecture promotes reusability and maintainability, with shared components potentially reused in the Electron desktop application.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Core Framework:** React 18.x with TypeScript 5.x for type-safe development
- **Styling:** TailwindCSS 3.x utility-first framework with custom theme configuration
- **Routing:** react-router-dom for client-side navigation and deep linking
- **State Management:** Zustand or Redux for global application state, React Query or SWR for server state caching
- **Form Handling:** react-hook-form with schema validation via Zod or Yup
- **HTTP Client:** axios or native fetch with interceptors for authentication token injection
- **Build Tooling:** Vite or Webpack for bundling, PostCSS for CSS processing

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

The web application consumes RESTful JSON APIs exposed by the Flask backend. All API communication occurs over HTTPS with JWT tokens in Authorization headers. API responses follow consistent JSON structures with standardized error formats. WebSocket connections (via socket.io or native WebSocket API) may provide real-time features such as notifications or live updates if required.

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

Client-side persistence uses browser localStorage for non-sensitive configuration and sessionStorage for temporary session data. Sensitive data (authentication tokens) stores in httpOnly cookies to prevent XSS attacks. Service workers (if PWA implemented) cache API responses and assets in IndexedDB for offline functionality.

**Scaling Considerations:**

The web application is entirely static after build, deployed to S3 and served via CloudFront CDN. Scaling occurs automatically through CloudFront's global edge network without application-level configuration. Code-splitting and lazy loading minimize initial bundle size. Tree-shaking eliminates unused code during production builds.

#### 5.2.1.2 React Native Mobile Application

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

React Native enables unified iOS and Android mobile applications from a single codebase, maximizing code reuse while delivering native performance. The application provides mobile-optimized user experiences with platform-specific UI patterns, gesture handling, and native module integration where web technologies are insufficient.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Core Framework:** React Native 0.73+ with TypeScript 5.x
- **Navigation:** react-navigation v6 with native stack navigators
- **Gesture Handling:** react-native-gesture-handler for performant touch interactions
- **Animations:** react-native-reanimated for 60fps native-driven animations
- **Safe Area Management:** react-native-safe-area-context for notch and dynamic island handling
- **HTTP Client:** axios with authentication interceptors
- **Platform APIs:** Native modules for camera, geolocation, push notifications, biometric authentication

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

Consumes identical RESTful APIs as web application, enabling code reuse for data fetching and state management logic. Platform-specific APIs accessed through React Native core modules and third-party native modules. Push notifications integrate via Firebase Cloud Messaging (Android) and Apple Push Notification Service (iOS).

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

Async Storage provides key-value persistence for application state and configuration. Secure storage libraries (react-native-keychain) store authentication tokens using platform keychain services (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore). SQLite (via react-native-sqlite-storage) provides relational storage if complex local data requirements emerge.

**Scaling Considerations:**

React Native applications scale through app store distribution rather than server infrastructure. Performance optimization focuses on bundle size reduction, native module bridging efficiency, and list virtualization for large datasets. Over-the-air updates (via CodePush or similar) enable rapid bug fixes without app store review cycles.

#### 5.2.1.3 Native iOS Application

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Native Swift-based iOS application provides maximum platform integration and performance for features requiring low-level iOS SDK access or superior user experience. Justified for scenarios where React Native's abstraction layer introduces unacceptable limitations or performance penalties.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Programming Language:** Swift 5.9+ with SwiftUI for declarative UI or UIKit for imperative control
- **Networking:** URLSession with Combine framework for reactive networking
- **Data Persistence:** Core Data for local database, UserDefaults for preferences, Keychain for secure storage
- **Dependency Management:** CocoaPods or Swift Package Manager
- **Authentication:** Auth0 iOS SDK for native authentication flows

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

Integrates with Flask backend APIs using URLSession with JWT authentication. Accesses iOS-specific features including HealthKit, ARKit, Core ML, SiriKit, WidgetKit, and App Clips. CloudKit integration provides iCloud synchronization if cross-device data persistence is required.

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

Core Data object graph management provides robust local persistence with automatic migration, conflict resolution, and CloudKit synchronization. Keychain stores authentication credentials with biometric protection (Touch ID, Face ID). File-based storage via FileManager for documents and media.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Distributed through Apple App Store with TestFlight for beta distribution. Performance optimization focuses on view hierarchy efficiency, memory management, and background task handling. App size reduction through on-demand resources and App Thinning.

#### 5.2.1.4 Native Android Application

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Kotlin-based native Android application delivers optimal Material Design implementation and platform-specific features unavailable through React Native. Provides deep Android ecosystem integration including widgets, live wallpapers, custom launchers, and system-level integrations.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Programming Language:** Kotlin 1.9+ with Jetpack Compose for modern declarative UI
- **Architecture:** MVVM pattern with ViewModels, LiveData, and Kotlin Coroutines
- **Networking:** Retrofit 2.x for REST API consumption with OkHttp client
- **Data Persistence:** Room database for SQLite abstraction, DataStore for preferences
- **Dependency Injection:** Dagger Hilt for dependency management
- **Authentication:** Auth0 Android SDK for native authentication flows

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

Consumes Flask backend REST APIs with Retrofit and coroutine-based async handling. Integrates Android-specific services including Google Play Services, Firebase (analytics, messaging, ML Kit), Android Auto, and WearOS companions.

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

Room provides type-safe SQLite database access with compile-time query verification and automated migrations. EncryptedSharedPreferences stores sensitive data using Android Keystore encryption. Files stored in application-specific directories with scoped storage compliance.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Distributed via Google Play Store with staged rollouts for gradual production deployment. APK/AAB size optimization through ProGuard code shrinking and resource optimization. Dynamic feature modules enable on-demand functionality delivery.

#### 5.2.1.5 macOS Native Application

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Objective-C AppKit-based macOS application provides native desktop experience with Mac-specific features including menu bar integration, system tray utilities, keyboard shortcuts, Touch Bar support, and Finder integration.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Programming Language:** Objective-C 2.0 with AppKit framework
- **UI Framework:** AppKit with Interface Builder or programmatic layout
- **Networking:** NSURLSession for HTTP communication
- **Data Persistence:** Core Data, NSUserDefaults, Keychain Services
- **Dependency Management:** CocoaPods or Swift Package Manager (Objective-C compatible)

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

REST API consumption via NSURLConnection with JWT authentication. Platform integrations include Notification Center, Share extensions, Quick Look, Spotlight indexing, and Services menu. AppleScript support enables automation and inter-application communication.

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

Core Data provides object persistence with SQLite backing store. Keychain Services secures authentication tokens with macOS keychain integration. iCloud Drive provides document storage and synchronization across user's Apple devices.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Distribution through Mac App Store or direct download with notarization. Application sandboxing and hardened runtime required for modern macOS security. Universal binaries support both Intel and Apple Silicon Macs.

#### 5.2.1.6 Electron Desktop Application

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Cross-platform desktop application leveraging web technologies (React, TypeScript, TailwindCSS) wrapped in Electron runtime. Provides consistent desktop experience across Windows, macOS, and Linux without platform-specific codebases. Reuses React web application components with desktop-specific enhancements.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Runtime:** Electron 28+ embedding Chromium and Node.js
- **UI Layer:** React 18+ with identical component library as web application
- **IPC Communication:** Electron IPC for main-renderer process communication
- **Native Integrations:** Node.js modules for file system, system notifications, auto-updates
- **Build System:** Electron Builder or Electron Forge for packaging

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

Consumes Flask backend APIs identically to web application. Node.js integration enables file system access, native dialogs, system tray, global keyboard shortcuts, and other OS-level features unavailable in browsers. IPC bridge connects renderer process (UI) with main process (Node.js).

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

Local storage and IndexedDB for browser-like persistence. Electron-store provides native key-value storage. node-keytar integrates with system credential managers (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service).

**Scaling Considerations:**

Distributed as platform-specific installers (DMG, EXE, AppImage, DEB) through direct download or auto-update server. Code signing required for each platform to prevent security warnings. Delta updates minimize download size for application updates.

### 5.2.2 API Gateway and Load Balancing

#### 5.2.2.1 AWS Application Load Balancer

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

The ALB serves as the single ingress point for all API traffic, performing SSL termination, request routing, health-based instance selection, and connection management. This managed AWS service eliminates the need for custom load balancer infrastructure while providing enterprise-grade reliability and automatic scaling.

**Technologies and Configuration:**

- **Load Balancer Type:** Application Load Balancer (Layer 7)
- **SSL/TLS:** AWS Certificate Manager provides free SSL certificates with automatic renewal
- **Target Groups:** ECS service-based target groups with dynamic port mapping
- **Health Checks:** HTTP health check endpoints on Flask services (`/health`, `/ready`)
- **Routing Rules:** Path-based and host-based routing with priority ordering
- **Sticky Sessions:** Cookie-based affinity if stateful sessions required (discouraged)

**Key Interfaces:**

Accepts HTTPS requests from all client applications on port 443. Routes requests to Flask backend instances registered in target groups on dynamic ports. Integrates with AWS WAF (Web Application Firewall) for additional security protection against common web exploits.

**Integration Points:**

- **Client Applications:** All platforms connect exclusively through ALB public DNS/IP
- **Backend Services:** ECS tasks register/deregister automatically via service discovery
- **CloudWatch:** Publishes metrics (request count, latency, target health, HTTP status codes)
- **Route 53:** DNS alias records point custom domain to ALB

**Scaling Considerations:**

ALB automatically scales to handle traffic volume without manual intervention. Cross-zone load balancing distributes requests across availability zones. Connection draining ensures graceful instance shutdown during deployments.

### 5.2.3 Application Layer Components

#### 5.2.3.1 Flask API Services

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Flask backend services implement all business logic, data validation, database operations, external service integration, and AI orchestration. The stateless design enables horizontal scaling by running multiple identical instances behind the load balancer without session affinity requirements.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Runtime:** Python 3.11+ for performance and modern language features
- **Web Framework:** Flask 3.x with Gunicorn WSGI server for production
- **Extensions:** Flask-CORS, Flask-JWT-Extended, Flask-RESTful, Flask-Limiter, Flask-Caching
- **Database Driver:** PyMongo for synchronous MongoDB operations, Motor for async (if needed)
- **Cache Client:** redis-py for Redis integration
- **Object Storage:** boto3 SDK for AWS S3 operations
- **AI Framework:** LangChain 0.1.x+ for LLM orchestration
- **Validation:** Pydantic for request/response schema validation
- **Background Jobs:** Celery with Redis broker for async task processing

**Key Interfaces and APIs:**

Exposes RESTful JSON APIs organized by resource domains:
- `/api/v1/auth/*` - Authentication and user management endpoints
- `/api/v1/users/*` - User profile and settings operations
- `/api/v1/ai/*` - AI-powered features and LLM interactions
- `/api/v1/files/*` - File upload/download and S3 pre-signed URL generation
- `/api/health` - Health check for load balancer
- `/api/metrics` - Prometheus-compatible metrics endpoint

**Data Persistence Requirements:**

No local persistence required due to stateless design. All persistent data stores in MongoDB. Temporary state (rate limiting, active sessions) stores in shared Redis instance. Application logs stream to CloudWatch Logs.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Horizontal scaling through ECS service auto-scaling based on CPU and memory metrics. Target scaling maintains average CPU utilization around 70%. Minimum 2 instances across availability zones for high availability. Maximum instances configured based on load testing and cost constraints. Connection pooling for database and Redis prevents connection exhaustion.

#### 5.2.3.2 LangChain AI Orchestration

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

LangChain integration module manages all interactions with large language models, vector databases, and AI-powered features. Abstracts provider-specific APIs behind unified interfaces, enabling model switching without application code changes. Implements prompt templates, chain composition, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and conversation memory management.

**Technologies and Frameworks:**

- **Core Framework:** LangChain Python library with provider-specific integrations
- **LLM Providers:** OpenAI SDK, Anthropic SDK, AWS Bedrock SDK
- **Vector Databases:** Pinecone, Weaviate, or Chroma clients
- **Embeddings:** OpenAI embeddings or open-source alternatives (sentence-transformers)
- **Document Loaders:** LangChain loaders for PDF, DOCX, HTML, Markdown
- **Text Splitters:** Recursive character and token-based splitters

**Key Interfaces:**

Flask routes invoke LangChain chains through Python function calls:
- `generate_response(prompt, context)` - Simple completion generation
- `conversational_chain(message, history)` - Stateful conversation
- `rag_query(question, knowledge_base)` - Retrieval-augmented generation
- `embed_documents(texts)` - Generate embeddings for semantic search
- `similarity_search(query, top_k)` - Find relevant context from vector store

**Integration Points:**

- **Flask Services:** Invoked by API endpoints requiring AI capabilities
- **MongoDB:** Stores conversation history, prompts, and responses for analysis
- **Vector Database:** Queries for semantic similarity, stores embeddings
- **LLM Providers:** Sends prompts, receives completions with streaming support
- **Redis:** Caches LLM responses for identical prompts (cost optimization)

**Scaling Considerations:**

LLM API calls represent potential bottleneck due to external service latency (1-10 seconds). Response caching in Redis dramatically reduces costs and improves performance for repeated queries. Asynchronous processing via Celery enables long-running AI tasks without blocking API responses. Circuit breaker pattern prevents cascade failures if LLM provider experiences downtime. Rate limiting prevents excessive API costs from runaway processes.

### 5.2.4 Caching Layer Components

#### 5.2.4.1 Redis Distributed Cache

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Redis provides sub-millisecond caching layer for frequently accessed data, session storage, rate limiting counters, and background job queue. Distributed architecture ensures all Flask instances access consistent cached data regardless of which instance handled previous requests.

**Technologies and Configuration:**

- **Service:** AWS ElastiCache for Redis (managed) for production, Docker container for development
- **Version:** Redis 7.x for latest features and security updates
- **Client Library:** redis-py with connection pooling
- **Data Structures:** Strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets leveraged based on use case
- **Persistence:** RDB snapshots and AOF logging for durability (configurable)
- **Eviction Policy:** LRU (Least Recently Used) for automatic memory management

**Key Use Cases:**

- **API Response Caching:** Cache GET endpoint responses with TTL (30 seconds to 1 hour)
- **Session Storage:** Store user session data keyed by session ID
- **Rate Limiting:** Counter-based rate limiting using INCR and EXPIRE
- **Temporary Tokens:** OTP codes, password reset tokens, email verification codes
- **Background Jobs:** Celery job queue and result storage
- **Pub/Sub:** Real-time notifications and messaging (if implemented)

**Integration Points:**

All Flask instances connect to shared ElastiCache Redis cluster. Flask-Caching extension provides decorator-based caching for routes and functions. Celery uses Redis as message broker and result backend. Manual Redis operations via redis-py for custom caching logic.

**Scaling Considerations:**

ElastiCache handles scaling through cluster mode with sharding or replication for read scalability. Read replicas distribute read load. Automatic failover ensures high availability. Memory sizing based on cache hit rate analysis and working set size.

### 5.2.5 Data Layer Components

#### 5.2.5.1 MongoDB Atlas Primary Database

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

MongoDB serves as the primary data persistence layer, storing all application data in flexible JSON-like BSON documents. Document model enables schema evolution without migrations, aggregation pipeline provides powerful analytics, and vector search capabilities support AI semantic search features.

**Technologies and Configuration:**

- **Service:** MongoDB Atlas (managed) on AWS in same region as application
- **Version:** MongoDB 7.x for Atlas Search vector capabilities
- **Deployment:** Replica set (3 nodes minimum) for high availability
- **Storage:** WiredTiger storage engine with compression
- **Backups:** Continuous backup with point-in-time recovery
- **Client:** PyMongo for synchronous operations, Motor for async if needed
- **ODM:** MongoEngine if ORM-style modeling preferred

**Key Collections and Data Models:**

- **Users:** User profiles, authentication metadata, preferences, roles
- **Sessions:** Active session tracking with TTL indexes for automatic expiration
- **AI Conversations:** Prompt/response pairs, conversation history, embeddings
- **Files:** Metadata for S3-stored files (key, size, type, owner, timestamps)
- **Audit Logs:** Comprehensive audit trail for compliance and debugging
- **Configuration:** Application settings, feature flags, system parameters

**Integration Points:**

Flask services connect via PyMongo driver with connection pooling. Database connection string stored in AWS Secrets Manager with automatic rotation. Change streams enable real-time notifications on data changes if required. Atlas Search provides full-text and vector search capabilities.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Horizontal scaling through sharding distributes data across multiple nodes based on shard key. Read preference configuration directs read traffic to secondary nodes. Indexes optimize query performance (compound, text, geospatial). Connection pooling prevents connection exhaustion (10-100 connections per Flask instance).

#### 5.2.5.2 AWS S3 Object Storage

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

S3 provides virtually unlimited object storage for user uploads, application assets, database backups, log archives, and generated reports. Integration with CloudFront enables global content delivery. Lifecycle policies automate cost optimization through transition to Glacier archival storage.

**Technologies and Configuration:**

- **Service:** AWS S3 with bucket-per-environment strategy
- **Client:** boto3 Python SDK for S3 operations
- **Encryption:** Server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) for all objects
- **Versioning:** Enabled for critical data buckets to prevent accidental deletion
- **Lifecycle Policies:** Transition to Glacier after 90 days (configurable per use case)
- **CORS:** Cross-origin configuration for direct browser uploads
- **Access Control:** IAM policies and bucket policies with least-privilege

**Key Buckets and Organization:**

- **User Uploads:** `{project}-uploads-{env}` - User-generated content with pre-signed URLs
- **Static Assets:** `{project}-assets-{env}` - Frontend builds served via CloudFront
- **Backups:** `{project}-backups-{env}` - MongoDB exports and system backups
- **Logs:** `{project}-logs-{env}` - Archived CloudWatch logs and application logs
- **ML Artifacts:** `{project}-ml-{env}` - AI model files and training data

**Integration Points:**

Flask generates pre-signed URLs for direct client-to-S3 uploads. CloudFront origins pull from S3 buckets for content delivery. Lambda functions (optional) trigger on S3 events for post-processing. IAM roles grant ECS tasks necessary S3 permissions without access keys.

**Scaling Considerations:**

S3 automatically scales to handle any request volume without configuration. Performance optimization through multi-part uploads for large files. CloudFront reduces origin load by caching frequently accessed objects at edge locations. Request rate optimization via key naming strategies to avoid hot partitions.

#### 5.2.5.3 AWS CloudFront CDN

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

CloudFront content delivery network distributes static assets and cacheable API responses from edge locations globally, reducing latency for geographically distributed users. SSL termination at edge locations protects content in transit.

**Technologies and Configuration:**

- **Service:** AWS CloudFront with multiple distributions per application component
- **Origins:** S3 buckets for static assets, ALB for API caching (if implemented)
- **SSL/TLS:** AWS Certificate Manager certificates with SNI
- **Cache Behaviors:** Path-based caching rules with TTL configuration
- **Invalidation:** Manual or automated cache invalidation on deployments
- **Edge Locations:** Global distribution across AWS edge network

**Key Distribution Configurations:**

- **Static Assets Distribution:** Serves frontend JavaScript, CSS, images from S3 with long TTL (1 year with versioned paths)
- **User Content Distribution:** Serves user uploads with signed URLs for access control
- **API Caching Distribution:** (Optional) Caches GET API responses at edge locations

**Integration Points:**

Frontend applications load from CloudFront distributions. S3 serves as origin for all distributions. Route 53 alias records point custom domains to CloudFront distributions. WAF rules protect distributions from common web attacks.

**Scaling Considerations:**

CloudFront automatically scales to handle traffic volume across global edge network. Cache hit rate monitoring identifies optimization opportunities. Regional edge caches provide additional caching layer for frequently accessed content not at edge locations.

### 5.2.6 Infrastructure and DevOps Components

#### 5.2.6.1 AWS ECS Container Orchestration

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

ECS manages Docker container lifecycle including deployment, scaling, health monitoring, and automated recovery. Service-based deployment model maintains desired container count with automatic replacement of unhealthy instances.

**Technologies and Configuration:**

- **Service:** AWS Elastic Container Service (Fargate launch type recommended)
- **Cluster:** ECS cluster spanning multiple availability zones
- **Task Definitions:** Container specifications including image, resources, environment
- **Services:** Maintain desired task count with load balancer integration
- **Service Discovery:** AWS Cloud Map for internal service-to-service communication
- **Auto Scaling:** Target tracking based on CPU/memory or custom CloudWatch metrics

**Key Service Configurations:**

- **Flask API Service:** 2-10 tasks with ALB target group integration, rolling deployment
- **Celery Workers:** 1-5 tasks without load balancer, consuming Redis queue
- **Scheduled Jobs:** Fargate scheduled tasks for periodic maintenance operations

**Integration Points:**

ECS pulls container images from ECR. ALB registers tasks as targets for traffic distribution. CloudWatch receives logs from task containers. Secrets Manager provides environment variables to tasks. IAM task roles grant AWS API permissions.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Fargate eliminates server management by providing serverless compute. Target tracking auto-scaling adjusts task count based on metrics. Scheduled scaling handles predictable traffic patterns. Cluster auto-scaling (if EC2 launch type) manages underlying infrastructure.

#### 5.2.6.2 Terraform Infrastructure Provisioning

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

Terraform defines all AWS infrastructure as declarative HCL code, enabling version-controlled infrastructure, reproducible environments, and automated provisioning. Pull request reviews provide change control for infrastructure modifications.

**Module Organization:**

- **Networking Module:** VPC, subnets (public/private), Internet Gateway, NAT Gateway, security groups, NACLs
- **Compute Module:** ECS cluster, task definitions, services, auto-scaling policies
- **Storage Module:** S3 buckets, CloudFront distributions, lifecycle policies
- **Database Module:** MongoDB Atlas configuration, Redis ElastiCache cluster
- **Security Module:** IAM roles and policies, Secrets Manager secrets, KMS keys
- **Monitoring Module:** CloudWatch dashboards, log groups, metric alarms, SNS topics
- **DNS Module:** Route 53 hosted zones and record sets

**Environment Strategy:**

Separate Terraform workspaces or directories for development, staging, and production environments. Environment-specific variable files configure sizing, redundancy, and feature flags. Remote state in S3 with DynamoDB locking prevents concurrent modifications.

**Integration Points:**

GitHub Actions workflows execute terraform plan on pull requests and terraform apply on merges. Terraform Cloud (optional) provides collaborative features and remote execution. Terraform providers for AWS, MongoDB Atlas, Auth0, and other services.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Modular design enables incremental infrastructure changes. State file organization prevents monolithic state that slows operations. Terraform workspaces enable isolated experimentation without environment conflicts.

#### 5.2.6.3 GitHub Actions CI/CD Pipeline

**Purpose and Responsibilities:**

GitHub Actions automates software delivery lifecycle including code quality checks, security scanning, container image builds, and environment deployments. Automated pipelines accelerate delivery velocity while maintaining quality through enforced gates.

**Workflow Organization:**

- **CI Workflow:** Runs on every push and pull request - linting, type checking, unit tests, coverage reports
- **Security Workflow:** Daily scheduled scan for dependency vulnerabilities using GitHub Dependabot
- **Build Workflow:** Triggered on tag creation - multi-stage Docker builds, security scanning, push to ECR
- **Deploy Development:** Triggered on merge to develop branch - automatic deployment to dev environment
- **Deploy Staging:** Triggered on merge to staging branch - automatic deployment with integration tests
- **Deploy Production:** Triggered on tag push with manual approval gate - blue-green deployment to production

**Quality Gates:**

All workflows must pass before merge permission granted. Minimum test coverage threshold (80%) enforced. Critical/high security vulnerabilities block deployment. Successful staging deployment required before production access.

**Integration Points:**

Workflows authenticate to AWS via OIDC (no long-lived credentials). Docker images push to ECR with semantic versioning tags. Terraform applies infrastructure changes through workflow automation. Slack or email notifications alert team of deployment status.

**Scaling Considerations:**

Self-hosted runners (optional) provide faster builds and access to private network resources. Matrix builds enable parallel testing across Python/Node versions. Workflow caching accelerates dependency installation. Reusable workflows eliminate duplication.

#### 5.2.7.2 Authentication Sequence Diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant Client as Client App
    participant Auth0 as Auth0 Platform
    participant ALB as Load Balancer
    participant Flask as Flask API
    participant MongoDB as MongoDB
    
    User->>Client: Initiate Login
    Client->>Auth0: Redirect to Auth0 Login
    Auth0->>User: Display Login Page
    User->>Auth0: Enter Credentials + MFA
    Auth0->>Auth0: Validate Credentials
    Auth0->>Client: Redirect with JWT Tokens
    Client->>Client: Store Access + Refresh Tokens
    
    Note over Client,Flask: Authenticated API Request
    
    Client->>ALB: API Request + JWT in Header
    ALB->>Flask: Route to Available Instance
    Flask->>Flask: Validate JWT Signature
    Flask->>Flask: Extract User Identity from Token
    Flask->>MongoDB: Query User Permissions
    MongoDB-->>Flask: Return User Roles
    Flask->>Flask: Authorize Request
    Flask->>MongoDB: Execute Business Logic
    MongoDB-->>Flask: Return Data
    Flask-->>ALB: JSON Response
    ALB-->>Client: Forward Response
    Client->>User: Display Data
    
    Note over Client,Auth0: Token Refresh Flow
    
    Client->>Client: Detect Token Expiration
    Client->>Auth0: Request New Access Token with Refresh Token
    Auth0->>Auth0: Validate Refresh Token
    Auth0-->>Client: Return New Access Token
    Client->>Client: Update Stored Token
```

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
```

#### 5.2.7.4 File Upload Sequence Diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor User
    participant Client as Client App
    participant Flask as Flask API

    S3->>S3: Validate Signature

    S3-->>Client: Confirm Upload Success

    Note over Client,Flask: Include S3 key, size, checksum

    MongoDB-->>Flask: Confirm Storage
    Flask-->>Client: Return File Record
    Client->>User: Display Upload Success
    
    Note over User,CDN: Later File Access
    
    User->>Client: Request File View
    Client->>Flask: GET /api/v1/files/{id}
    Flask->>MongoDB: Query File Metadata
    MongoDB-->>Flask: Return S3 Key + Permissions
    Flask->>Flask: Check User Permissions
    Flask->>CDN: Generate CDN URL or Signed S3 URL
    Flask-->>Client: Return File URL
    Client->>CDN: GET File from CloudFront
    CDN->>S3: Fetch from Origin (if cache miss)
    S3-->>CDN: Return File
    CDN-->>Client: Serve Cached File
    Client->>User: Display File
```
