### 6.3.2 API Design

#### 6.3.2.1 Protocol Specifications

**Primary Communication Protocol: RESTful API over HTTPS**

The system implements REST (Representational State Transfer) architectural style over HTTPS with TLS 1.3 encryption for all client-server communication. This approach provides standardized, stateless, and cacheable interactions that align with industry best practices and enable broad client platform compatibility.

**Communication Architecture:**

```
Client Applications → Application Load Balancer (TLS Termination) → Flask Backend (HTTP/HTTPS)
                                ↓
                    All API endpoints follow REST principles
                    Standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)
                    JSON request/response payloads
                    Stateless authentication via JWT tokens
```

**HTTP Method Semantics:**

| Method | Idempotent | Safe | Purpose | Response Codes |
|--------|------------|------|---------|----------------|
| **GET** | Yes | Yes | Retrieve resources without side effects | 200, 404, 403 |
| **POST** | No | No | Create new resources | 201, 400, 409 |
| **PUT** | Yes | No | Replace entire resource | 200, 404, 400 |
| **PATCH** | No | No | Partial resource update | 200, 404, 400 |
| **DELETE** | Yes | No | Remove resource | 204, 404, 403 |

**API Endpoint Organization:**

```
Base URL: https://api.newnov6.com

Authentication Endpoints:
  POST   /api/v1/auth/signup          - User registration
  POST   /api/v1/auth/login           - User authentication
  POST   /api/v1/auth/logout          - Session termination
  POST   /api/v1/auth/refresh         - Token refresh
  POST   /api/v1/auth/password-reset  - Password reset request

User Management Endpoints:
  GET    /api/v1/users/{user_id}      - Retrieve user profile
  PATCH  /api/v1/users/{user_id}      - Update user profile
  DELETE /api/v1/users/{user_id}      - Delete user account
  GET    /api/v1/users/{user_id}/preferences - Get preferences
  PUT    /api/v1/users/{user_id}/preferences - Update preferences

AI Orchestration Endpoints:
  POST   /api/v1/ai/query             - Submit AI query
  GET    /api/v1/ai/conversations     - List conversations
  GET    /api/v1/ai/conversations/{id} - Retrieve conversation
  DELETE /api/v1/ai/conversations/{id} - Delete conversation

File Management Endpoints:
  POST   /api/v1/files/request-upload - Request pre-signed URL
  POST   /api/v1/files/confirm-upload - Confirm upload completion
  GET    /api/v1/files                - List user files
  GET    /api/v1/files/{file_id}      - Retrieve file metadata
  DELETE /api/v1/files/{file_id}      - Delete file

System Endpoints:
  GET    /api/health                  - Health check
  GET    /api/metrics                 - Operational metrics
```

**Standard Request Headers:**

```http
Authorization: Bearer {jwt_access_token}
Content-Type: application/json
Accept: application/json
X-Request-ID: {unique_request_identifier}
User-Agent: {client_application_identifier}
```

{

    "resource_specific_data": "value"
  },

    "timestamp": "2024-11-06T15:30:45.123Z",

{

#### 6.3.2.2 Authentication Methods

**Primary: OAuth 2.0 with OpenID Connect via Auth0**

The system delegates authentication to Auth0, a managed identity platform that implements OAuth 2.0 authorization framework and OpenID Connect authentication layer. This approach offloads security-critical operations to specialized infrastructure with dedicated security expertise, as documented in Section 3.5.1.1 (Third-Party Services).

**Authentication Flow Diagram:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client App
    participant Auth0 as Auth0 Platform
    participant Flask as Flask API
    participant Redis
    participant MongoDB

    User->>Client: Click "Login"
    Client->>Auth0: Redirect to Auth0 login page
    Auth0->>User: Display login form + MFA
    User->>Auth0: Credentials + MFA code
    Auth0->>Auth0: Validate credentials
    
    alt Authentication Success
        Auth0->>Client: Authorization code
        Client->>Flask: Exchange code for tokens
        Flask->>Auth0: Validate authorization code
        Auth0->>Flask: JWT access token + refresh token
        Flask->>Redis: Store refresh token
        Flask->>Client: Access token + refresh token
        
        Client->>Flask: API request with JWT
        Flask->>Flask: Validate JWT signature
        Flask->>Flask: Check token blacklist
        Flask->>MongoDB: Query user permissions
        MongoDB->>Flask: User data
        Flask->>Client: API response
    else Authentication Failure
        Auth0->>User: Error message
    end
```

**JWT Token Structure:**

```json
{
  "header": {
    "alg": "RS256",
    "typ": "JWT",
    "kid": "auth0_key_id_abc123"
  },
  "payload": {
    "iss": "https://tenant.auth0.com/",
    "sub": "auth0|user_1234567890",
    "aud": "https://api.newnov6.com",
    "iat": 1699282245,
    "exp": 1699285845,
    "azp": "client_application_id",
    "scope": "openid profile email",
    "permissions": [
      "read:data",
      "write:data",
      "access:ai"
    ]
  },
  "signature": "base64_encoded_signature"
}
```

**Token Lifecycle Management:**

| Token Type | TTL | Storage Location | Refresh Strategy | Security Measures |
|------------|-----|------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Access Token** | 15-60 minutes | Client memory (not localStorage) | Automatic on expiry | Short TTL, signature validation |
| **Refresh Token** | 30 days | Secure storage (httpOnly cookie) | Manual user re-auth after expiry | Long TTL, rotation on use |
| **Blacklist** | Match token TTL | Redis (until expiry) | On logout/security events | Token JTI stored in Redis set |

**Token Validation Process:**

```python
# Flask middleware for JWT validation
from functools import wraps
from flask import request, g, jsonify
import jwt
import redis

redis_client = redis.Redis(host='redis-endpoint', port=6379)

def require_auth(func):
    """JWT authentication middleware"""
    @wraps(func)
    def decorated_function(*args, **kwargs):
        # 1. Extract token from Authorization header
        auth_header = request.headers.get('Authorization')
        if not auth_header or not auth_header.startswith('Bearer '):
            return jsonify({"error": "Missing or invalid authorization header"}), 401
        
        token = auth_header.split(' ')[1]
        
        try:
            # 2. Retrieve Auth0 public keys (cached in Redis)
            public_key = get_cached_auth0_public_key()
            
            # 3. Validate JWT signature and claims
            decoded_token = jwt.decode(
                token,
                public_key,
                algorithms=['RS256'],
                audience='https://api.newnov6.com',
                issuer='https://tenant.auth0.com/'
            )
            
            # 4. Check token blacklist (logout/revocation)
            token_jti = decoded_token.get('jti')
            if redis_client.exists(f"blacklist:{token_jti}"):
                return jsonify({"error": "Token has been revoked"}), 401
            
            # 5. Extract user context
            g.user = {
                'user_id': decoded_token['sub'],
                'email': decoded_token.get('email'),
                'permissions': decoded_token.get('permissions', [])
            }
            
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
            
        except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
            return jsonify({"error": "Token has expired"}), 401
        except jwt.InvalidTokenError as e:
            return jsonify({"error": f"Invalid token: {str(e)}"}), 401
    
    return decorated_function
```

**Multi-Factor Authentication Support:**

Auth0 provides multiple MFA methods as documented in Section 3.5.1.1:

- SMS-based OTP (Time-based One-Time Password)
- Authenticator App (Google Authenticator, Authy)
- Push Notifications (Auth0 Guardian mobile app)
- Email OTP
- Biometric Authentication (platform-native)

#### 6.3.2.3 Authorization Framework

**Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)**

The system implements role-based authorization with fine-grained permissions stored in JWT token claims and validated on every API request, as documented in Section 5.4.4 (Cross-Cutting Concerns - Authentication and Authorization).

**User Roles and Permissions:**

| Role | Permission Scope | Use Cases |
|------|-----------------|-----------|
| **Admin** | Full system access, user management, configuration | System administrators, support team |
| **Power User** | Extended features (AI, analytics, exports, unlimited uploads) | Premium subscribers, enterprise users |
| **Standard User** | Basic operations, limited AI usage, read own data | Free-tier users, individual accounts |
| **Read-Only** | View-only access, no modifications | Auditors, compliance officers, reporting |

**Permission Granularity (Resource:Action Pattern):**

```
Authentication & User Management:
  - users:read          View user profiles
  - users:write         Modify user profiles
  - users:delete        Delete user accounts
  - admin:users         Manage all users (admin only)

AI Features:
  - ai:query            Submit AI queries
  - ai:history          Access conversation history
  - ai:export           Export conversations

File Management:
  - files:upload        Upload files
  - files:read          Access files
  - files:delete        Delete files
  - files:share         Share files with others

System Administration:
  - admin:config        Modify system configuration
  - admin:audit         Access audit logs
  - admin:metrics       View system metrics
```

**Authorization Enforcement:**

```python
def require_permission(permission):
    """Permission-based authorization decorator"""
    def decorator(func):
        @wraps(func)
        def decorated_function(*args, **kwargs):
            # User context set by @require_auth middleware
            user_permissions = g.user.get('permissions', [])
            
            if permission not in user_permissions:
                return jsonify({
                    "error": {
                        "code": "INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS",
                        "message": f"Required permission: {permission}",
                        "required": permission,
                        "current": user_permissions
                    }
                }), 403
            
            return func(*args, **kwargs)
        return decorated_function
    return decorator

#### Usage example: AI query endpoint
@app.route('/api/v1/ai/query', methods=['POST'])
@require_auth  # JWT validation
@require_permission('ai:query')  # Permission check
def ai_query():
    """AI query endpoint - requires 'ai:query' permission"""
    user_id = g.user['user_id']
    query_text = request.json.get('query')
    
#### Process AI query...
    response = langchain_service.process_query(user_id, query_text)
    
    return jsonify({"status": "success", "data": response})
```

#### 6.3.2.4 Rate Limiting Strategy

**Implementation: Flask-Limiter with Redis Storage Backend**

Rate limiting protects the API from abuse, ensures fair resource allocation, and controls costs for metered external services (LLM APIs). As documented in Section 6.1.2.4, Redis serves as the distributed rate limit counter storage.

**Rate Limit Configuration:**

| Endpoint Category | Rate Limit | Scope | Enforcement |
|------------------|------------|-------|-------------|
| **General API** | 60 requests/minute | Per user | Redis counter with 60s TTL |
| **Authentication** | 5 attempts/5 minutes | Per IP address | Brute-force protection |
| **AI Queries** | Tier-based (10-100/hour) | Per user | Cost control |
| **File Uploads** | 20 uploads/hour | Per user | Storage cost control |

**Rate Limit Response Headers:**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-RateLimit-Limit: 60
X-RateLimit-Remaining: 42
X-RateLimit-Reset: 1699282800
```

**Rate Limit Exceeded Response:**

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED",
    "message": "Too many requests. Please try again later.",
    "retry_after_seconds": 45,
    "limit": 60,
    "window": "1 minute"
  },
  "metadata": {
    "timestamp": "2024-11-06T15:30:45.123Z",
    "request_id": "req_abc123xyz"
  }
}
```

**Implementation Example:**

```python
from flask_limiter import Limiter
from flask_limiter.util import get_remote_address
import redis

#### Redis-backed rate limiter
limiter = Limiter(
    app=app,
    key_func=get_remote_address,  # Rate limit by IP address
    storage_uri="redis://redis-endpoint:6379",
    default_limits=["60 per minute"]  # Global default
)

#### Per-endpoint rate limiting
@app.route('/api/v1/auth/login', methods=['POST'])
@limiter.limit("5 per 5 minutes")  # Stricter limit for login
def login():
    """Login endpoint with brute-force protection"""
#### Authentication logic...
    pass

#### User-specific rate limiting
def get_user_id():
    """Extract user ID from JWT for user-based rate limiting"""
    if hasattr(g, 'user'):
        return g.user['user_id']
    return get_remote_address()

@app.route('/api/v1/ai/query', methods=['POST'])
@require_auth
@limiter.limit("10 per hour", key_func=get_user_id)  # Standard user limit
def ai_query():
    """AI query with user-specific rate limit"""
    # Check for Power User role (higher limit)
    if 'power_user' in g.user.get('roles', []):
        # Override with higher limit for Power Users
        limiter.limit("100 per hour")(lambda: None)()
    
    # Process AI query...
    pass
```

#### 6.3.2.5 API Versioning Approach

**Strategy: URL Path Versioning**

The API implements version identification through URL path prefixes (`/api/v1/`, `/api/v2/`), enabling backward-compatible evolution and multiple version support during transition periods, as documented in Section 6.1.3.1 (Service Communication Patterns).

**Versioning Policy:**

- **Current Version**: v1 (initial release)
- **Version Format**: `/api/v{major_version}/`
- **Deprecation Notice**: 6-month advance notification before version sunset
- **Multiple Version Support**: Old versions supported during transition period
- **Breaking Changes**: Trigger new major version (v1 → v2)
- **Non-Breaking Changes**: Deployed to existing version without version increment

**Version Migration Path:**

```
Phase 1: New version released (v2 alongside v1)
  - /api/v1/* continues working (full support)
  - /api/v2/* available (new features, breaking changes)
  - Documentation updated with migration guide

Phase 2: Deprecation notice (Month 0-6)
  - Response header added: X-API-Version-Deprecated: true
  - Response header: X-API-Version-Sunset: 2025-06-01
  - Email notifications to developers using v1
  - Migration guide and code examples published

Phase 3: Grace period (Month 6-9)
  - /api/v1/* returns 410 Gone for new clients
  - Existing clients continue working with warnings
  - Support team assists with migrations

Phase 4: Version sunset (Month 9+)
  - /api/v1/* returns 410 Gone for all requests
  - Only /api/v2/* operational
```

**Version-Specific Response Headers:**

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
X-API-Version: v1
X-API-Version-Deprecated: false
X-API-Version-Sunset: null
Link: </api/v2/users/123>; rel="successor-version"
```

#### 6.3.2.6 API Documentation Standards

**Documentation Tools (Planned Implementation):**

| Tool | Purpose | Access |
|------|---------|--------|
| **OpenAPI 3.0 Specification** | Machine-readable API definition | `/api/openapi.json` |
| **Swagger UI** | Interactive API documentation | `/api/docs` |
| **Postman Collections** | Pre-configured API requests for testing | Developer portal |
| **Code Examples** | Python, JavaScript, cURL examples | Documentation site |

**Documentation Content Requirements:**

Each API endpoint documentation includes:

1. **Endpoint Overview**: URL pattern, HTTP method, brief description
2. **Authentication**: Required permissions and token scopes
3. **Request Specification**:
   - Path parameters with types and constraints
   - Query parameters with defaults and validation rules
   - Request body schema with examples
4. **Response Specification**:
   - Success response (200, 201, 204) with schema and example
   - Error responses (400, 401, 403, 404, 500) with scenarios
5. **Rate Limits**: Applicable rate limits and throttling behavior
6. **Versioning**: Version introduced, deprecation status
7. **Examples**: Complete request/response examples for common scenarios

### 6.3.3 Message Processing

#### 6.3.3.1 Background Job Processing Architecture

**Implementation: Celery with Redis Message Broker**

The system implements asynchronous task processing using Celery distributed task queue with Redis as the message broker, enabling long-running operations to execute without blocking API requests, as documented in Section 6.1.2.2 (Flask API Application) and Section 6.1.2.4 (Redis Distributed Cache).

**Architecture Diagram:**

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "API Layer"
        Flask[Flask API<br/>Web Requests]
    end
    
    subgraph "Message Broker"
        Redis[(Redis<br/>Task Queue<br/>Result Backend)]
    end
    
    subgraph "Worker Layer"
        Worker1[Celery Worker 1<br/>ECS Task]
        Worker2[Celery Worker 2<br/>ECS Task]
        WorkerN[Celery Worker N<br/>ECS Task]
    end
    
    subgraph "External Services"
        SMTP[Email Service]
        S3[Amazon S3]
        MongoDB[(MongoDB)]
    end
    
    Flask -->|Queue Task| Redis
    Redis -->|Poll Tasks| Worker1
    Redis -->|Poll Tasks| Worker2
    Redis -->|Poll Tasks| WorkerN
    
    Worker1 --> SMTP
    Worker1 --> S3
    Worker1 --> MongoDB
    Worker2 --> SMTP
    Worker2 --> S3
    Worker2 --> MongoDB
    
    style Redis fill:#DC382D,color:#fff
    style Worker1 fill:#90EE90
    style Worker2 fill:#90EE90
```

**Use Cases for Async Processing:**

- **Email Notifications**: Welcome emails, password resets, alerts (avoid blocking API response)
- **Data Exports**: Large CSV/PDF generation (computationally expensive)
- **Batch Data Processing**: Bulk updates, data migrations (long-running operations)
- **File Processing**: Image resizing, document parsing, thumbnail generation
- **Scheduled Jobs**: Report generation, data cleanup, backups (time-based triggers)
- **AI Conversation Archival**: Moving old conversations to S3 Glacier (periodic maintenance)

**Celery Configuration:**

```python
from celery import Celery
from celery.schedules import crontab

#### Initialize Celery
celery = Celery(
    'newnov_backend',
    broker='redis://redis-endpoint:6379/0',
    backend='redis://redis-endpoint:6379/0'
)

#### Configuration
celery.conf.update(
#### Task routing to dedicated queues
    task_routes={
        'app.tasks.email.*': {'queue': 'email'},
        'app.tasks.ai.*': {'queue': 'ai'},
        'app.tasks.export.*': {'queue': 'export'},
        'app.tasks.file.*': {'queue': 'files'},
    },
    
#### Result expiration (7 days)
    result_expires=604800,
    
#### Task acknowledgment after execution (reliability)
    task_acks_late=True,
    
#### Worker prefetch multiplier (1 = fair distribution)
    worker_prefetch_multiplier=1,
    
#### Task time limits
    task_soft_time_limit=300,  # 5 minutes soft limit (SoftTimeLimitExceeded exception)
    task_time_limit=600,       # 10 minutes hard limit (SIGKILL)
)

#### Scheduled tasks (Celery Beat)
celery.conf.beat_schedule = {
    'archive-old-conversations-daily': {
        'task': 'app.tasks.archive_old_conversations',
        'schedule': crontab(hour=2, minute=0),  # Daily at 2 AM UTC
    },
    'export-audit-logs-daily': {
        'task': 'app.tasks.export_audit_logs_to_s3',
        'schedule': crontab(hour=3, minute=0),  # Daily at 3 AM UTC
    },
    'generate-analytics-report-daily': {
        'task': 'app.tasks.generate_daily_analytics',
        'schedule': crontab(hour=4, minute=0),  # Daily at 4 AM UTC
    },
}

**Task Definition Example:**

```python
from celery import Task
import smtplib

@celery.task(bind=True, max_retries=3, default_retry_delay=60)
def send_welcome_email(self, user_email, user_name):
    """Send welcome email to new user"""
    try:
        # Send email via SMTP
        send_email(
            to=user_email,
            subject="Welcome to NewNov_6_1",
            body=f"Hello {user_name}, welcome to our platform!"
        )
        return {"status": "success", "email": user_email}
        
    except smtplib.SMTPException as exc:
        # Retry with exponential backoff
        # Retry delays: 60s, 120s, 240s (2^retry_count * default_retry_delay)
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=60 * (2 ** self.request.retries))

#### Queue task from Flask API
@app.route('/api/v1/auth/signup', methods=['POST'])
def signup():
    """User registration endpoint"""
#### Create user synchronously
    user = create_user(request.json)
    
#### Queue welcome email asynchronously (non-blocking)
    send_welcome_email.delay(user.email, user.name)
    
    return jsonify({"status": "success", "user_id": user.id}), 201
```

**ECS Service Configuration:**

| Service | Task Count | Auto-Scaling Trigger | Priority |
|---------|-----------|---------------------|----------|
| **Flask API** | 2-20 tasks | CPU utilization > 70% | High |
| **Celery Worker** | 1-5 tasks | Queue depth > 100 jobs | Medium |
| **Celery Beat** | 1 task (singleton) | N/A (always 1) | Low |

#### 6.3.3.2 Event Processing Patterns

**Pattern: Task Queue (Asynchronous Work Distribution)**

The primary event processing pattern implements a task queue where API requests enqueue jobs to Redis, and distributed Celery workers process jobs asynchronously with automatic retry and failure handling.

**Processing Flow:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Flask as Flask API
    participant Redis as Redis Queue
    participant Celery as Celery Worker
    participant Service as External Service
    participant CW as CloudWatch

    Client->>Flask: API Request
    Flask->>Flask: Process synchronous logic
    Flask->>Redis: Queue background task
    Redis-->>Flask: Task ID
    Flask->>Client: Response (with task_id)
    
    Note over Redis,Celery: Async Processing
    
    Celery->>Redis: Poll for tasks
    Redis->>Celery: Dequeue task
    Celery->>Service: Execute task
    
    alt Success
        Service->>Celery: Success response
        Celery->>Redis: Store result
        Celery->>CW: Log success metric
    else Failure
        Service->>Celery: Error response
        Celery->>Celery: Retry logic (exponential backoff)
        Celery->>Redis: Requeue task (if retries remaining)
        Celery->>CW: Log failure metric
    end
```

**Idempotency Pattern:**

All background tasks designed to be idempotent (safe to retry without side effects):

```python
@celery.task(bind=True, max_retries=3)
def process_file_upload(self, file_id):
    """Process uploaded file (idempotent)"""
    # Check if already processed (idempotency)
    file_metadata = db.files.find_one({"file_id": file_id})
    if file_metadata.get("processed") == True:
        return {"status": "already_processed", "file_id": file_id}
    
    try:
        # Process file (thumbnail generation, metadata extraction, etc.)
        result = process_file(file_metadata['s3_key'])
        
        # Update database with processed flag (atomic operation)
        db.files.update_one(
            {"file_id": file_id, "processed": {"$ne": True}},  # Only update if not processed
            {"$set": {"processed": True, "processing_result": result}}
        )
        
        return {"status": "success", "file_id": file_id}
        
    except Exception as exc:
        raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=60 * (2 ** self.request.retries))
```

#### 6.3.3.3 Message Queue Architecture

**Redis as Lightweight Message Broker**

Redis serves as the message broker due to its sub-millisecond latency, simple deployment model, and sufficient reliability for non-critical background jobs, as documented in Section 6.1.2.4 (Redis Distributed Cache).

**Queue Configuration:**

| Queue Name | Purpose | Priority | Worker Pool |
|-----------|---------|----------|-------------|
| **default** | General background tasks | Normal | All workers |
| **email** | Email notification delivery | High | Dedicated email workers |
| **ai** | AI-related processing (embeddings, archival) | Normal | AI-optimized workers |
| **export** | Data export generation | Low | Export-specific workers |
| **files** | File processing (thumbnails, parsing) | Normal | File processing workers |

**Persistence and Reliability:**

- **RDB Snapshots**: Hourly snapshots to S3 (recoverable within 1 hour)
- **AOF Logging**: Optional append-only file for higher durability (disabled for performance)
- **Multi-AZ Deployment**: Primary in us-east-1a, replica in us-east-1b (automatic failover)
- **Failure Scenario**: If Redis fails, tasks queued during downtime are lost (acceptable for non-critical jobs)
- **Critical Tasks**: Store task metadata in MongoDB before queuing (can be requeued after Redis recovery)

**Monitoring and Auto-Scaling:**

```python

import boto3

cloudwatch = boto3.client('cloudwatch')

def publish_queue_depth_metric():
    """Publish queue depth to CloudWatch for auto-scaling"""
    # Get queue depth from Redis
    queue_depth = redis_client.llen('celery')
    
    cloudwatch.put_metric_data(
        Namespace='Application/BackgroundJobs',
        MetricData=[{
            'MetricName': 'QueueDepth',
            'Value': queue_depth,
            'Unit': 'Count',
            'Dimensions': [
                {'Name': 'Queue', 'Value': 'celery'},
                {'Name': 'Environment', 'Value': 'production'}
            ]
        }]
    )

#### ECS auto-scaling policy triggered by queue depth:
#### - Queue depth > 100: Scale out (add worker)
#### - Queue depth < 10: Scale in (remove worker)
```

#### 6.3.3.4 Error Handling Strategy

**Retry Logic with Exponential Backoff**

All background tasks implement automatic retry with exponential backoff to handle transient failures gracefully:

**Retry Configuration:**

```
Maximum Retries: 3-5 (configurable per task)
Base Delay: 60 seconds
Backoff Multiplier: 2x
Jitter: ±20% random variation

Retry Timeline:
  Attempt 1: Immediate
  Attempt 2: 60s ± 12s
  Attempt 3: 120s ± 24s
  Attempt 4: 240s ± 48s
  Final attempt: 480s ± 96s
```

**Dead Letter Queue:**

Tasks that exhaust all retries move to a dead letter queue for manual investigation:

```python
@celery.task(bind=True, max_retries=3)
def risky_operation(self, data):
    """Task with dead letter queue for failures"""
    try:
        # Attempt operation
        result = perform_operation(data)
        return result
    except Exception as exc:
        if self.request.retries < self.max_retries:
            # Retry
            raise self.retry(exc=exc, countdown=60 * (2 ** self.request.retries))
        else:
            # All retries exhausted - move to dead letter queue
            dead_letter_entry = {
                "task_id": self.request.id,
                "task_name": self.name,
                "args": self.request.args,
                "kwargs": self.request.kwargs,
                "exception": str(exc),
                "retries": self.request.retries,
                "timestamp": datetime.utcnow()
            }
            db.dead_letter_queue.insert_one(dead_letter_entry)
            
            # Alert operations team
            cloudwatch.put_metric_data(
                Namespace='Application/BackgroundJobs',
                MetricData=[{
                    'MetricName': 'TaskFailures',
                    'Value': 1,
                    'Unit': 'Count'
                }]
            )
            
            raise  # Re-raise for logging
```

**Monitoring and Alerting:**

- **CloudWatch Metrics**: Task success/failure rates, queue depth, processing time
- **Alerts**: Sustained high failure rate (> 10% over 5 minutes)
- **Dead Letter Queue**: Dashboard showing failed tasks requiring manual intervention

#### 6.3.4.2 Auth0 Integration Details

**OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow**

Auth0 implements the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow for secure authentication with support for social identity providers, multi-factor authentication, and enterprise SSO, as documented in Section 6.1.2.9 (Auth0 Authentication Platform).

**Token Validation (Stateless):**

```python
import jwt
import requests
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def get_auth0_public_keys():
    """Retrieve and cache Auth0 public keys (JWKS)"""
    # Fetch public keys from Auth0 JWKS endpoint
    jwks_url = f"https://{AUTH0_DOMAIN}/.well-known/jwks.json"
    response = requests.get(jwks_url)
    jwks = response.json()
    
    # Convert to PyJWT format
    public_keys = {}
    for key in jwks['keys']:
        kid = key['kid']
        public_keys[kid] = jwt.algorithms.RSAAlgorithm.from_jwk(json.dumps(key))
    
    return public_keys

def validate_jwt_token(token):
    """Validate JWT token from Auth0"""
    try:
        # Decode header to get key ID
        unverified_header = jwt.get_unverified_header(token)
        kid = unverified_header['kid']
        
        # Get corresponding public key
        public_keys = get_auth0_public_keys()
        public_key = public_keys[kid]
        
        # Validate token
        decoded_token = jwt.decode(
            token,
            public_key,
            algorithms=['RS256'],
            audience='https://api.newnov6.com',
            issuer=f'https://{AUTH0_DOMAIN}/'
        )
        
        return decoded_token
        
    except jwt.ExpiredSignatureError:
        raise AuthenticationError("Token has expired")
    except jwt.InvalidAudienceError:
        raise AuthenticationError("Invalid token audience")
    except jwt.InvalidIssuerError:
        raise AuthenticationError("Invalid token issuer")
    except Exception as e:
        raise AuthenticationError(f"Token validation failed: {str(e)}")
```

**Configuration Requirements:**

- Auth0 tenant creation and domain configuration
- Application registration for each platform (web, mobile, API)
- JWT signing algorithm: RS256 (RSA with SHA-256)
- Custom domain for branded authentication flows (optional)
- Role and permission definitions mapped to JWT claims
- Social identity provider credentials (Google, GitHub, Microsoft)

#### 6.3.4.3 MongoDB Atlas Integration

**Connection Pattern: PyMongo with Connection Pooling**

The Flask application connects to MongoDB Atlas using PyMongo driver with optimized connection pooling for performance and reliability, as documented in Section 6.2.4.1 (Database Design - Replica Set Configuration).

**Connection Configuration:**

```python
from pymongo import MongoClient, WriteConcern, ReadPreference

#### Production connection configuration
client = MongoClient(
    connection_string,
    
#### Connection pool settings
    minPoolSize=10,              # Always maintain 10 warm connections
    maxPoolSize=100,             # Allow burst to 100 connections
    maxIdleTimeMS=30000,         # Close idle connections after 30 seconds
    waitQueueTimeoutMS=5000,     # Fail fast if no connection available
    serverSelectionTimeoutMS=5000,
    
#### Write concern and read preference
    w="majority",                # Write to majority of replica set
    readPreference="primaryPreferred",  # Primary for reads, fallback to secondary
    
#### TLS/SSL configuration
    tls=True,
    tlsAllowInvalidCertificates=False,
    
#### Application identification
    appName="newnov-flask-backend-prod"
)

db = client.newnov_db
```

**Automatic Failover:**

- **3-Node Replica Set**: Primary in us-east-1a, secondaries in us-east-1b and us-east-1c
- **Failure Detection**: 10-second heartbeat interval
- **Election Time**: 10-30 seconds to elect new primary
- **Application Impact**: Automatic reconnection to new primary (PyMongo handles transparently)
- **Data Loss**: Zero data loss with `w="majority"` write concern

#### 6.3.4.4 AWS Services Integration

**S3 Direct Upload Pattern (Pre-Signed URLs)**

To minimize backend load and leverage S3's superior bandwidth, the system implements direct client-to-S3 uploads using pre-signed URLs, as documented in Section 6.1.2.6 (S3 Object Storage).

**Pre-Signed URL Flow:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Flask as Flask API
    participant S3 as Amazon S3
    participant MongoDB

    Client->>Flask: POST /api/v1/files/request-upload<br/>{filename, content_type}
    Flask->>Flask: Validate user permissions
    Flask->>Flask: Generate S3 key
    Flask->>S3: Generate pre-signed URL<br/>(15-minute expiry)
    S3-->>Flask: Pre-signed URL
    Flask->>Client: {pre_signed_url, file_id, upload_url}
    
    Note over Client,S3: Direct Upload (bypasses Flask)
    
    Client->>S3: PUT file to pre-signed URL
    S3->>S3: Validate signature & expiry
    S3->>Client: Upload success (200 OK)
    
    Client->>Flask: POST /api/v1/files/confirm-upload<br/>{file_id, s3_key}
    Flask->>MongoDB: Store file metadata
    MongoDB-->>Flask: Confirmation
    Flask->>Client: {status: success, file_id}
```

**Implementation:**

```python
import boto3
from datetime import timedelta

s3_client = boto3.client('s3', region_name='us-east-1')

@app.route('/api/v1/files/request-upload', methods=['POST'])
@require_auth
def request_file_upload():
    """Generate pre-signed URL for direct S3 upload"""
    user_id = g.user['user_id']
    filename = request.json.get('filename')
    content_type = request.json.get('content_type')
    
    # Generate unique S3 key
    file_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    s3_key = f"uploads/{user_id}/{datetime.utcnow().strftime('%Y/%m/%d')}/{file_id}_{filename}"
    
    # Generate pre-signed URL (15-minute expiry)
    presigned_url = s3_client.generate_presigned_url(
        'put_object',
        Params={
            'Bucket': 'newnov-uploads-prod',
            'Key': s3_key,
            'ContentType': content_type
        },
        ExpiresIn=900  # 15 minutes
    )
    
    return jsonify({
        "status": "success",
        "data": {
            "file_id": file_id,
            "upload_url": presigned_url,
            "s3_key": s3_key,
            "expires_in": 900
        }
    })

@app.route('/api/v1/files/confirm-upload', methods=['POST'])
@require_auth
def confirm_file_upload():
    """Store file metadata after successful upload"""
    user_id = g.user['user_id']
    file_id = request.json.get('file_id')
    s3_key = request.json.get('s3_key')
    
    # Verify file exists in S3
    try:
        head_response = s3_client.head_object(
            Bucket='newnov-uploads-prod',
            Key=s3_key
        )
        
        # Store metadata in MongoDB
        file_metadata = {
            "file_id": file_id,
            "user_id": user_id,
            "s3_key": s3_key,
            "s3_bucket": "newnov-uploads-prod",
            "filename": os.path.basename(s3_key),
            "content_type": head_response['ContentType'],
            "size_bytes": head_response['ContentLength'],
            "created_at": datetime.utcnow(),
            "is_public": False
        }
        
        db.files.insert_one(file_metadata)
        
        return jsonify({"status": "success", "file_id": file_id})
        
    except s3_client.exceptions.NoSuchKey:
        return jsonify({"error": "File upload not confirmed"}), 400
```

**Benefits:**

- Offloads file transfer from application tier (reduces infrastructure costs)
- Leverages S3's superior bandwidth and reliability
- Enables multi-part resumable uploads for large files
- Supports client-side progress tracking
- Reduces backend latency and load

#### 6.3.4.5 LLM Provider Integration (via LangChain)

**Integration Architecture:**

LangChain provides the AI orchestration framework, abstracting LLM provider APIs and managing prompt engineering, chain composition, and retrieval-augmented generation workflows, as documented in Section 6.1.2.3 (LangChain AI Orchestration Layer).

**LangChain Integration Benefits:**

- **Provider Agnostic**: Switch between OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS Bedrock without code changes
- **Fallback Providers**: If primary provider fails, automatically failover to alternative
- **Prompt Management**: Template-based prompt engineering with variable substitution
- **Chain Composition**: Sequential and parallel chain orchestration for complex workflows
- **Memory Management**: Conversation context and history tracking

**AI Request Flow:**

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Client
    participant Flask
    participant LangChain
    participant VectorDB as Vector Database
    participant LLM as OpenAI/Anthropic
    participant MongoDB
    participant Redis

    Client->>Flask: POST /api/v1/ai/query<br/>{query, conversation_id}
    Flask->>Flask: Validate JWT & permissions
    Flask->>Redis: Check cache (query hash)
    
    alt Cache Hit
        Redis->>Flask: Cached AI response
        Flask->>Client: Return cached response
    else Cache Miss
        Redis-->>Flask: Cache miss
        Flask->>LangChain: Process AI query
        LangChain->>VectorDB: Semantic search for context
        VectorDB->>LangChain: Relevant documents (RAG)
        LangChain->>LangChain: Construct prompt from template
        LangChain->>LLM: Send prompt
        LLM->>LangChain: AI response
        LangChain->>Flask: Processed response
        Flask->>MongoDB: Store conversation
        Flask->>Redis: Cache response (5 min TTL)
        Flask->>Client: Return AI response
    end
```

**Implementation Example:**

```python
from langchain.chat_models import ChatOpenAI, ChatAnthropic
from langchain.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain.vectorstores import Pinecone
from langchain.embeddings import OpenAIEmbeddings

#### Initialize LLM providers
openai_llm = ChatOpenAI(
    model="gpt-4-turbo-preview",
    temperature=0.7,
    openai_api_key=os.environ.get('OPENAI_API_KEY')
)

anthropic_llm = ChatAnthropic(
    model="claude-3-opus-20240229",
    temperature=0.7,
    anthropic_api_key=os.environ.get('ANTHROPIC_API_KEY')
)

#### Prompt template
prompt_template = ChatPromptTemplate.from_messages([
    ("system", "You are a helpful AI assistant. Use the following context to answer the user's question: {context}"),
    ("user", "{user_query}")
])

#### Vector database for RAG
vectorstore = Pinecone.from_existing_index(
    index_name="newnov-embeddings",
    embedding=OpenAIEmbeddings()
)

@app.route('/api/v1/ai/query', methods=['POST'])
@require_auth
@require_permission('ai:query')
def ai_query():
    """AI query endpoint with RAG"""
    user_id = g.user['user_id']
    query = request.json.get('query')
    conversation_id = request.json.get('conversation_id')
    
    # Check cache
    cache_key = f"ai:query:{hashlib.md5(query.encode()).hexdigest()}"
    cached_response = redis_client.get(cache_key)
    if cached_response:
        return jsonify(json.loads(cached_response))
    
    try:
        # RAG: Retrieve relevant context from vector database
        context_docs = vectorstore.similarity_search(query, k=3)
        context = "\n\n".join([doc.page_content for doc in context_docs])
        
        # Construct prompt
        prompt = prompt_template.format_messages(
            context=context,
            user_query=query
        )
        
        # Query LLM with circuit breaker
        response = query_llm_with_fallback(prompt)
        
        # Store conversation in MongoDB
        conversation_entry = {
            "conversation_id": conversation_id or str(uuid.uuid4()),
            "user_id": user_id,
            "messages": [
                {"role": "user", "content": query, "timestamp": datetime.utcnow()},
                {"role": "assistant", "content": response, "timestamp": datetime.utcnow()}
            ],
            "llm_provider": "openai",
            "model": "gpt-4-turbo-preview",
            "tokens_used": estimate_tokens(query + response),
            "created_at": datetime.utcnow(),
            "updated_at": datetime.utcnow()
        }
        db.ai_conversations.insert_one(conversation_entry)
        
        # Cache response (5 minutes)
        redis_client.setex(cache_key, 300, json.dumps({"response": response}))
        
        return jsonify({"status": "success", "data": {"response": response}})
        
    except Exception as e:
        return jsonify({"error": str(e)}), 500

def query_llm_with_fallback(prompt):
    """Query LLM with circuit breaker and fallback"""
    # Circuit breaker pattern (implemented via pybreaker library)
    try:
        response = openai_llm(prompt)
        return response.content
    except Exception as primary_error:
        # Fallback to Anthropic if OpenAI fails
        try:
            response = anthropic_llm(prompt)
            return response.content
        except Exception as fallback_error:
            raise Exception(f"All LLM providers failed: {primary_error}, {fallback_error}")
```

**Circuit Breaker Configuration:**

| Provider | Failure Threshold | Timeout Duration | Success Threshold |
|----------|------------------|------------------|-------------------|
| **OpenAI API** | 5 consecutive failures | 60 seconds | 1 success |
| **Anthropic API** | 5 consecutive failures | 60 seconds | 1 success |
| **Vector Database** | 5 consecutive failures | 60 seconds | 1 success |

| **MongoDB Atlas** | 99.95% (M10+) | <50ms queries | Based on cluster tier | Read replicas, cache |

        Flask->>Client: 401 Unauthorized

### 6.3.6 Integration Security and Resilience

#### 6.3.6.1 Network Security Architecture

**Defense in Depth:**

The integration architecture implements multiple layers of network security to protect against unauthorized access and data breaches, as documented in Section 6.1.7.2 (Data Redundancy - Network Topology).

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Public Internet"
        Internet[Public Internet]
    end
    
    subgraph "AWS VPC - 10.0.0.0/16"
        subgraph "Public Subnets - DMZ"
            ALB[Application Load Balancer<br/>Security Group: 443 from 0.0.0.0/0]
        end
        
        subgraph "Private Subnets - Application Tier"
            Flask[Flask ECS Tasks<br/>Security Group: 8000 from ALB only]
        end
        
        subgraph "Private Subnets - Data Tier"
            Redis[ElastiCache Redis<br/>Security Group: 6379 from Flask only]
        end
    end
    
    subgraph "MongoDB Atlas VPC"
        MongoDB[(MongoDB Cluster<br/>VPC Peering<br/>IP Allowlist)]
    end
    
    Internet -->|HTTPS:443| ALB
    ALB -->|HTTP:8000| Flask
    Flask -->|Redis:6379| Redis
    Flask -->|MongoDB:27017| MongoDB
    
    Internet -.X blocked.-> Flask
    Internet -.X blocked.-> Redis
    Internet -.X blocked.-> MongoDB
    
    style ALB fill:#87CEEB
    style Flask fill:#90EE90
    style Redis fill:#FFB6C1
    style MongoDB fill:#4DB33D,color:#fff
```

**Security Layers:**

1. **VPC Network Isolation**: Private subnets for application and data tiers (no direct internet access)
2. **Security Groups (Stateful Firewall)**: Allow only required ports from specific sources
3. **MongoDB Atlas IP Allowlist**: Only Flask subnet CIDR ranges can connect
4. **VPC Peering**: Direct private connection between AWS VPC and MongoDB Atlas (no internet traversal)
5. **TLS Encryption**: All connections encrypted in transit (TLS 1.2+)

#### 6.3.6.2 Data Encryption

**Encryption at Rest:**

| Service | Encryption Method | Key Management |
|---------|------------------|----------------|
| **MongoDB Atlas** | AES-256 automatic | MongoDB managed keys |
| **Redis ElastiCache** | AES-256 | AWS KMS customer managed key |
| **S3 Objects** | SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS | AWS KMS customer managed key |
| **EBS Volumes** | AES-256 | AWS KMS customer managed key |

**Encryption in Transit:**

- Client ↔ ALB: TLS 1.3 with modern cipher suites
- ALB ↔ Flask: TLS 1.2+ within VPC
- Flask ↔ MongoDB: TLS 1.3 via MongoDB wire protocol
- Flask ↔ Redis: TLS 1.2+ (AWS ElastiCache)
- Flask ↔ S3: HTTPS TLS 1.2+
- Flask ↔ Auth0: HTTPS TLS 1.2+
- Flask ↔ LLM Providers: HTTPS TLS 1.2+

#### 6.3.6.3 Resilience Patterns

**Circuit Breaker Pattern:**

Prevents cascading failures when external dependencies become unreliable, as documented in Section 6.1.5.1 (Resilience and Fault Tolerance).

**Circuit States:**

```
Closed (Normal): All requests pass through, failures counted
   ↓ (5 consecutive failures)
Open (Fail Fast): Requests rejected immediately, no external calls
   ↓ (60-second timeout)
Half-Open (Testing): Single test request sent to evaluate recovery
   ↓ (success → Closed, failure → Open)
```

**Retry with Exponential Backoff:**

```
Retry Sequence:
  Attempt 1: Immediate
  Attempt 2: 1 second (±0.2s jitter)
  Attempt 3: 2 seconds (±0.4s jitter)
  Attempt 4: 4 seconds (±0.8s jitter)
  Attempt 5: 8 seconds (±1.6s jitter)
  Maximum: 16 seconds (±3.2s jitter)
```

**Graceful Degradation:**

| Dependency Failure | Degradation Strategy | User Impact |
|-------------------|---------------------|-------------|
| **Redis Down** | Direct database queries | Increased latency (no errors) |
| **MongoDB Down** | Serve stale cache data | Data may be outdated warning |
| **LLM Provider Down** | Return cached responses or queue | AI features delayed message |
| **S3 Down** | Queue uploads for retry | Upload queued notification |
| **Auth0 Down** | Use cached public keys | Existing sessions work, new logins fail |

## 6.4 Security Architecture

### 6.4.1 Security Architecture Overview

#### 6.4.1.1 Security Philosophy and Design Principles

The NewNov_6_1 system implements a **defense-in-depth security architecture** that leverages managed security services, industry best practices, and multiple overlapping security layers to protect user data and system integrity. The security design prioritizes risk reduction through delegation of authentication-critical operations to specialized platforms while maintaining comprehensive control over authorization, data protection, and audit capabilities.

**Architectural Context:** As documented in Section 1.3 (System Overview), the system is currently in initialization phase with no implementation code. All security architecture specifications represent planned architecture documented in the Technical Specification, awaiting implementation.

**Core Security Principles:**

| Principle | Implementation | Security Benefit |
|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| **Least Privilege** | Role-based access control with minimal necessary permissions per role | Limits blast radius of compromised accounts |
| **Defense in Depth** | Multiple overlapping security layers (WAF, security groups, encryption, authentication, authorization, audit logging) | No single point of failure in security posture |
| **Secure by Default** | Encryption enabled, secure configurations, deny-by-default access controls | Eliminates security misconfigurations |
| **Zero Trust** | Every request validated and authenticated regardless of source | Prevents lateral movement after breach |

**Key Security Decisions:**

As documented in Section 5.3.4 (Technical Decisions - Security Architecture), critical security architecture decisions include:

1. **Auth0 Managed Authentication**: Delegation of authentication to specialized identity platform eliminates custom authentication vulnerabilities and provides enterprise-grade security features including MFA, breach detection, and compliance certifications

2. **Stateless JWT Authentication**: JWT-based authentication enables horizontal scaling without session storage while maintaining strong security through cryptographic signature validation

3. **Multi-Layer Network Security**: VPC isolation combined with security groups, network ACLs, and WAF provides comprehensive network protection

4. **AWS KMS Key Management**: Centralized encryption key management with automatic rotation and audit trails

5. **Comprehensive Audit Logging**: 90-day hot storage plus 7-year archival meets compliance requirements (SOX, GDPR Article 30)

---

### 6.4.2 Authentication Framework

#### 6.4.2.1 Identity Management

**Auth0 Managed Identity Platform**

The system delegates all authentication operations to Auth0, implementing OAuth 2.0 authorization framework and OpenID Connect authentication layer. This architectural decision offloads security-critical operations to dedicated infrastructure with professional security expertise, as documented in Section 5.3.4.1 (Technical Decisions - Auth0 Selection).

**Identity Provider Configuration:**

| Component | Implementation | Security Feature |
|-----------|----------------|------------------|
| **Identity Provider** | Auth0 tenant (e.g., `newnov6.auth0.com`) | SOC 2, ISO 27001, GDPR, HIPAA certified |
| **Password Hashing** | Argon2 (Auth0 default) | Industry-leading password hashing algorithm |
| **Breach Detection** | Have I Been Pwned integration | Prevents compromised password usage |
| **Bot Protection** | CAPTCHA and behavioral analysis | Prevents automated attacks |

**Supported Authentication Methods:**

- Email/password credentials with Argon2 password hashing
- Social identity providers (Google, GitHub, Microsoft)
- Enterprise SSO (SAML, OIDC) for business customers
- Passwordless authentication (email magic links, SMS OTP)

**User Registration and Profile Storage:**

User data follows a dual-storage pattern separating authentication concerns from application data:

- **Auth0**: Core authentication data (email, password hash, verification status, Auth0 user ID)
- **MongoDB**: Application-specific user data (preferences, roles, permissions, profile information)
- **Synchronization**: User ID (subject claim from JWT) links Auth0 identity to MongoDB user document

#### 6.4.2.2 Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA)

**Supported MFA Methods:**

| Method | Implementation | Security Level | User Experience |
|--------|---------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **Authenticator App** | TOTP (Google Authenticator, Authy, Microsoft Authenticator) | High | App generates 6-digit code |
| **Push Notification** | Auth0 Guardian mobile app | High | User approves/denies login |
| **SMS OTP** | Time-based one-time password via SMS | Medium | User receives 6-digit code |
| **Email OTP** | One-time code sent to registered email | Medium | User enters code from email |

**MFA Enforcement Policies:**

```
Configuration per User Role:
- Admin Role: MFA REQUIRED (cannot access admin features without MFA)
- Power User: MFA OPTIONAL (strongly recommended)
- Standard User: MFA OPTIONAL (user choice)
- Read-Only: MFA OPTIONAL

Risk-Based Adaptive MFA (Auth0 Anomaly Detection):
- New device login → MFA challenge
- Unusual geographic location → MFA challenge
- Velocity anomaly (multiple rapid attempts) → MFA challenge + temporary account lock
- Breached password detected → Forced password change + MFA challenge
```

#### 6.4.2.3 Session Management

**Token-Based Session Architecture:**

The system implements **stateless JWT-based authentication** eliminating server-side session storage, as documented in Section 5.3.2.2 (Technical Decisions - JWT Stateless Authentication). All session context resides in cryptographically signed JWT tokens validated on each request.

**Token Types and Lifecycle:**

| Token Type | Purpose | Lifetime | Storage Location | Refresh Mechanism |
|-----------|---------|----------|------------------|-------------------|
| **Access Token** | API authentication | 15-60 minutes | Client memory (not localStorage) | Automatic refresh using refresh token |
| **Refresh Token** | Access token renewal | 30 days | Secure httpOnly cookie (web), secure enclave (mobile) | Manual re-authentication after expiry |
| **ID Token** | User profile information | 15-60 minutes | Client storage | Not used for API authentication |

**JWT Access Token Structure:**

Access tokens contain all necessary authentication context enabling stateless validation:

- **Header**: Algorithm (RS256), token type, key ID for signature verification
- **Payload**: Issuer (Auth0 tenant), subject (user ID), audience (API identifier), expiration, permissions, user email, roles
- **Signature**: RSA-256 cryptographic signature for tamper detection

**Token Validation Process:**

As documented in Section 6.1.2.9 (Core Services - Auth0 Integration), Flask validates Auth0-issued JWTs without making API calls for each request:

1. **Extract Token**: Read JWT from Authorization header
2. **Signature Verification**: Validate token signature using cached Auth0 public key (Redis 24-hour TTL)
3. **Claims Validation**: Verify issuer, audience, expiration
4. **Blacklist Check**: Verify token not revoked (Redis lookup)
5. **Extract Context**: Retrieve user ID, roles, permissions for request processing

**Performance Optimization:**
- Public keys cached in Redis (24-hour TTL) reduce Auth0 API calls to once per day
- Local cryptographic signature verification adds <1ms overhead per request
- Stateless design enables unlimited horizontal scaling without session storage

#### 6.4.2.4 Token Handling and Revocation

**Token Refresh Flow:**

When access tokens expire, clients automatically refresh using refresh tokens without re-authentication:

1. Client detects access token expiration (401 TOKEN_EXPIRED response)
2. Client sends refresh token to Auth0 `/oauth/token` endpoint
3. Auth0 validates refresh token (signature, expiration, user account status)
4. Auth0 returns new access token (optionally rotated refresh token)
5. Client retries original request with new access token
6. Request succeeds transparently (user unaware of token refresh)

**Token Revocation (Logout & Security Events):**

Immediate token revocation implemented through Redis blacklist pattern:

1. Revoke refresh tokens via Auth0 API (prevents new access tokens)
2. Blacklist active access tokens in Redis (TTL matches token expiration)
3. Delete session records from MongoDB
4. Log security event to audit trail

**Token Security Best Practices:**

| Security Measure | Implementation | Protection Against |
|-----------------|----------------|---------------------|
| **httpOnly Cookies** | Tokens in httpOnly cookies (web) | XSS attacks stealing tokens |
| **Secure Flag** | Cookies transmitted only over HTTPS | Man-in-the-middle token interception |
| **SameSite Attribute** | SameSite=Lax or Strict | Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) |
| **Short Access Token TTL** | 15-60 minute expiration | Limits exposure if compromised |

#### 6.4.2.5 Password Policies

**Password Requirements:**

```
Minimum Password Strength:
- Length: Minimum 8 characters, recommended 12+ characters
- Complexity Requirements:
  ✓ At least 1 lowercase letter (a-z)
  ✓ At least 1 uppercase letter (A-Z)
  ✓ At least 1 number (0-9)
  ✓ At least 1 special character (!@#$%^&*)

Prohibited Patterns:
  ✗ Common passwords (blocked via 10M+ password dictionary)
  ✗ Sequential characters (abc123, qwerty)
  ✗ User personal information (email, name in password)
  ✗ Breached passwords (checked against Have I Been Pwned database)

Password History:
- Last 5 passwords cannot be reused

Password Expiration Policy:
- Admin accounts: 90-day forced password change
- Standard users: No forced expiration (follows NIST guidelines)
```

**Account Lockout Policy:**

```
Brute Force Protection:
- Threshold: 10 failed login attempts within 5 minutes
- Action: Account temporarily locked for 15 minutes
- Notification: Email sent to user about lockout (security alert)
- Unlock Options:
  1. Wait 15 minutes (automatic unlock)
  2. Use "Unlock Account" email link (immediate unlock)
  3. Contact support for manual unlock

Progressive Delays (Rate Limiting):
- Failed login #1-3: No delay
- Failed login #4-6: 2-second delay before response
- Failed login #7-9: 5-second delay before response
- Failed login #10+: Account lockout triggered
```

### 6.4.3 Authorization System

#### 6.4.3.1 Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)

**Role Definitions:**

| Role | Target Users | Permission Scope | Use Cases |
|------|-------------|------------------|-----------|
| **Admin** | System administrators, support engineers | Full system access including user management, configuration, audit logs | System operations, troubleshooting, compliance audits |
| **Power User** | Premium subscribers, enterprise customers | Extended features: unlimited AI queries, advanced analytics, data exports, API access | Power users requiring advanced capabilities |
| **Standard User** | Free-tier users, individual accounts | Basic features: limited AI queries (10/hour), file uploads (20/hour), read own data | Standard application usage |
| **Read-Only** | Auditors, compliance officers, reporting tools | View-only access to system data, no modifications | Compliance reviews, reporting dashboards |

**Role Assignment:**
- **Default Role:** Standard User (assigned on signup)
- **Role Promotion:** Admin can upgrade users (Standard → Power User, Standard → Admin)
- **Role Persistence:** Roles stored in MongoDB users collection and Auth0 user metadata
- **JWT Claims:** Roles included in JWT token for stateless authorization

#### 6.4.3.2 Permission Management

**Permission Granularity (Resource:Action Pattern):**

Permissions follow a structured `resource:action` pattern enabling fine-grained access control:

```
User Management Permissions:
- users:read              View user profiles
- users:write             Modify user profiles
- users:delete            Delete user accounts
- users:roles:manage      Assign/modify user roles

AI Feature Permissions:
- ai:query                Submit AI queries
- ai:history              Access conversation history
- ai:export               Export conversations
- ai:advanced             Access advanced features (RAG, custom models)

File Management Permissions:
- files:upload            Upload files to S3
- files:read              Access files
- files:delete            Delete files
- files:share             Share files with other users

System Administration Permissions:
- admin:users             Full user management
- admin:config            Modify system configuration
- admin:audit             Access audit logs
- admin:metrics           View system metrics
```

**Permission-to-Role Mapping:**

- **Admin**: All permissions (users, AI, files, admin)
- **Power User**: users:read/write, ai:*, files:*, no admin permissions
- **Standard User**: users:read/write, ai:query/history, files:upload/read/delete
- **Read-Only**: users:read, ai:history, files:read only

#### 6.4.3.3 Resource Authorization

**Document-Level Access Control:**

As documented in Section 6.3 (Integration Architecture), the system enforces ownership validation ensuring users can only access their own resources unless granted Admin privileges:

```
Authorization Flow:
1. JWT Validation: Verify token signature and expiration
2. Permission Check: Verify user has required permission (e.g., files:delete)
3. Ownership Validation: Verify user owns resource OR has Admin role
4. Authorization Passed: Execute business logic
```

**Query-Level Filtering:**

Database queries automatically scoped to user's resources:

- **Admin/Read-Only**: Query returns all documents (no filtering)
- **Standard Users**: Query filtered by `user_id` (see only own data)
- **Implementation**: Application adds `{user_id: current_user_id}` filter to MongoDB queries

#### 6.4.3.4 Policy Enforcement Points

**Multi-Layer Authorization Enforcement:**

```
Layer 1: API Gateway (ALB + WAF)
- Rate limiting (DDoS protection)
- IP allowlisting/blocklisting
- Request size limits

Layer 2: Flask Middleware (@require_auth decorator)
- JWT signature validation
- Token expiration check
- Token blacklist verification
- Extract user context

Layer 3: Route-Level Authorization (@require_permission decorator)
- Permission existence check
- Return 403 Forbidden if permission missing

Layer 4: Resource-Level Authorization (function logic)
- Ownership validation
- Admin bypass for privileged users
- Audit logging of access attempts

Layer 5: Database-Level Access Control
- MongoDB RBAC roles
- Application service account has readWrite role only
- Principle of least privilege
```

#### 6.4.3.5 Audit Logging

**Comprehensive Audit Trail:**

As documented in Section 6.2.7.4 (Database Design - Audit Mechanisms), all significant security and data access events are logged to MongoDB `audit_logs` collection with 90-day hot retention and 7-year archival for compliance.

**Audit Log Schema:**

| Field | Description | Purpose |
|-------|-------------|---------|
| `log_id` | Unique log identifier | Audit trail reference |
| `user_id` | User who performed action | Attribution |
| `action_type` | CREATE, UPDATE, DELETE, ACCESS, LOGIN, LOGOUT | Event classification |
| `resource_type` | Type of resource affected | Resource tracking |
| `resource_id` | Specific resource identifier | Resource identification |
| `timestamp` | Action timestamp | Chronological ordering |
| `ip_address` | Client IP address | Forensic analysis |
| `changes` | Before/after values (for UPDATE) | Change tracking |
| `status` | SUCCESS, FAILURE, PARTIAL | Outcome tracking |

**Events Requiring Audit Logging:**

- **Authentication Events**: Login (success/failure), logout, password change, MFA enable/disable, account lockout
- **Authorization Events**: Permission denied (403), role changes, admin impersonation
- **Data Access Events**: File downloads, user data exports, bulk operations
- **Data Modification Events**: Profile updates, file uploads/deletions, configuration changes, account deletion (GDPR)
- **Security Events**: Suspicious login attempts, token revocation, security policy violations

**Audit Log Retention Policy:**

| Environment | Hot Storage (MongoDB) | Archive Storage (S3 Glacier) | Total Retention | Compliance Basis |
|-------------|----------------------|------------------------------|-----------------|------------------|
| **Production** | 90 days | 7 years | 7 years total | SOX, GDPR Article 30 |
| **Staging** | 30 days | None | 30 days | Development/testing |
| **Development** | 7 days | None | 7 days | Development/testing |

### 6.4.4 Data Protection

#### 6.4.4.1 Encryption Standards

**Encryption at Rest:**

As documented in Section 6.2.7.2 (Database Design - Privacy Controls), all data stores implement AES-256 encryption:

| Data Store | Encryption Method | Key Management | Compliance |
|-----------|------------------|----------------|------------|
| **MongoDB Atlas** | AES-256 automatic encryption | MongoDB managed keys or AWS KMS customer managed keys | GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2, ISO 27001 |
| **Redis ElastiCache** | AES-256 encryption at rest | AWS KMS customer managed key | GDPR, PCI DSS |
| **Amazon S3** | Server-side encryption (SSE-KMS) | AWS KMS customer managed key | GDPR, HIPAA, SOC 2 |
| **EBS Volumes** | AES-256 encryption | AWS KMS customer managed key | GDPR, HIPAA |
| **Backup Snapshots** | AES-256 encryption | AWS KMS customer managed key | GDPR, HIPAA |

**Encryption in Transit:**

All network communications encrypted using TLS:

- **Client ↔ ALB**: TLS 1.3 (preferred), TLS 1.2 (fallback) with modern cipher suites
- **ALB ↔ Flask**: TLS 1.2+ within VPC
- **Flask ↔ MongoDB**: TLS 1.3 via VPC peering
- **Flask ↔ Redis**: TLS 1.2+ within VPC
- **Flask ↔ External APIs**: HTTPS TLS 1.2+ (Auth0, LLM providers, S3)

**TLS Configuration:**

| Connection | TLS Version | Cipher Suites | Certificate Authority |
|-----------|-------------|---------------|----------------------|
| **Client → ALB** | TLS 1.3, TLS 1.2 | ECDHE-RSA-AES256-GCM-SHA384, ECDHE-RSA-AES128-GCM-SHA256 | AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) |
| **Internal Services** | TLS 1.2+ | AES256-GCM-SHA384 | AWS-managed or self-signed |

#### 6.4.4.2 Key Management

**AWS KMS (Key Management Service) Architecture:**

```
Encryption Key Hierarchy:

Root Key (AWS KMS Customer Master Key - CMK)
├── Data Encryption Key for MongoDB
├── Data Encryption Key for Redis
├── Data Encryption Key for S3 Buckets
├── Data Encryption Key for EBS Volumes
└── Data Encryption Key for Secrets Manager

Key Rotation:
- Customer Master Keys (CMKs): Automatic annual rotation
- Data Encryption Keys (DEKs): Rotated on each encryption operation
- Backup Keys: Retained for decrypting old data after rotation
```

**Key Access Control:**

IAM policies control which AWS services and roles can use encryption keys:
- **ECS Task Role**: Decrypt permission for secrets and encrypted data
- **S3 Service**: GenerateDataKey and Decrypt permissions for bucket encryption
- **MongoDB Atlas**: Decrypt permission via VPC peering integration

#### 6.4.4.3 Data Masking Rules

**Sensitive Data Scrubbing in Logs:**

As documented in Section 6.2.7.2 (Database Design - Privacy Controls), the system automatically scrubs sensitive data from all log messages before emission:

**Scrubbed Patterns:**
- Passwords (any field named "password")
- Social Security Numbers (###-##-####)
- Credit card numbers (#### #### #### ####)
- API keys (api_key=...)
- Tokens (bearer/token=...)
- Email addresses

**API Response Data Masking:**

Role-based field masking in API responses:
- **Admin**: See all fields unmasked
- **Non-Admin**: Email partially masked (first 3 chars + ***@domain), phone numbers fully masked (***-***-****)

#### 6.4.4.4 Secure Communication

**VPC Network Architecture:**

As documented in Section 5.3.4.2 (Technical Decisions - Network Security), the system implements defense-in-depth network security:

**Network Isolation:**

- **Public Subnets** (10.0.1.0/24, 10.0.2.0/24): ALB and NAT Gateway only
- **Private Subnets - App Tier** (10.0.10.0/24, 10.0.11.0/24): Flask instances (no internet access)
- **Private Subnets - Data Tier** (10.0.20.0/24, 10.0.21.0/24): Redis ElastiCache (no internet access)
- **MongoDB Atlas VPC**: Separate VPC with VPC peering connection (no internet traversal)

**Security Group Rules:**

| Security Group | Inbound Rules | Outbound Rules | Purpose |
|---------------|---------------|----------------|---------|
| **ALB** | 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 | 8000 to Flask SG | Public HTTPS ingress |
| **Flask** | 8000 from ALB SG | 6379 to Redis SG, 27017 to MongoDB, 443 to internet (via NAT) | Application tier |
| **Redis** | 6379 from Flask SG | None | Data tier cache |

**MongoDB Atlas Network Security:**

- **VPC Peering**: Private connection between AWS VPC and MongoDB Atlas VPC
- **IP Allowlist**: Only VPC CIDR block (10.0.0.0/16) permitted to connect
- **TLS Encryption**: All connections require TLS 1.3
- **No Public Internet**: MongoDB cluster not exposed to public internet

#### 6.4.4.5 Compliance Controls

**GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation) Compliance:**

As documented in Section 6.2.7.1 (Database Design - Data Retention Rules), the system implements comprehensive GDPR compliance:

| GDPR Requirement | Implementation | Evidence |
|-----------------|----------------|----------|
| **Right to Access (Art. 15)** | User data export API endpoint | MongoDB users, files, conversations collections |
| **Right to Erasure (Art. 17)** | Complete data deletion with anonymized audit logs | GDPR deletion logs in `gdpr_deletions` collection |
| **Right to Rectification (Art. 16)** | User profile update API | Audit logs record all updates |
| **Right to Data Portability (Art. 20)** | JSON format data export | Machine-readable structured export |
| **Data Minimization (Art. 5)** | Collect only email, name, user-generated content | Database schema review |
| **Consent Management (Art. 7)** | Explicit consent checkboxes | User preferences in MongoDB |
| **Data Protection by Design (Art. 25)** | Encryption, access controls, audit logging | Architecture documentation |

**SOC 2 Type II Compliance:**

| Trust Service Criteria | Implementation | Evidence |
|------------------------|----------------|----------|
| **Security (CC6)** | Encryption, access controls, MFA, firewalls | Security architecture documentation |
| **Availability (A1)** | Multi-AZ deployment, auto-scaling, 99.9% uptime SLA | CloudWatch metrics |
| **Processing Integrity (PI1)** | Input validation, error handling, audit logging | Code reviews, testing |
| **Confidentiality (C1)** | Data classification, encryption, access controls | Data protection documentation |

**HIPAA Readiness:**

*Note: HIPAA compliance requires Business Associate Agreements (BAA) with AWS and MongoDB Atlas, available on enterprise plans.*

Architecture implements HIPAA-ready safeguards:
- **Administrative Safeguards**: Access controls, workforce training, incident response
- **Physical Safeguards**: AWS data center physical security (SOC 2 certified)
- **Technical Safeguards**: Encryption, access controls, audit logging, transmission security

### 6.4.5 Security Architecture Diagrams

#### 6.4.5.1 Authentication Flow Diagram

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Client as Client App
    participant Auth0 as Auth0 Platform
    participant Flask as Flask API
    participant Redis
    participant MongoDB

    User->>Client: Click "Login"
    Client->>Auth0: Redirect to Auth0 login page
    Auth0->>User: Display login form + MFA
    User->>Auth0: Credentials + MFA code
    Auth0->>Auth0: Validate credentials
    
    alt Authentication Success
        Auth0->>Client: Authorization code
        Client->>Auth0: Exchange code for tokens
        Auth0->>Client: JWT access token + refresh token
        Client->>Client: Store tokens securely
        
        Client->>Flask: API request with JWT Bearer token
        Flask->>Redis: Check cached Auth0 public keys
        alt Cache Hit
            Redis->>Flask: Cached public keys
        else Cache Miss
            Flask->>Auth0: Fetch public keys (JWKS)
            Auth0->>Flask: Public keys
            Flask->>Redis: Cache public keys (24h TTL)
        end
        
        Flask->>Flask: Validate JWT signature + claims
        Flask->>Redis: Check token blacklist
        alt Token Not Blacklisted
            Flask->>MongoDB: Query user permissions
            MongoDB->>Flask: User data
            Flask->>Flask: Authorize request
            Flask->>Client: API response (200 OK)
        else Token Blacklisted
            Flask->>Client: 401 Unauthorized (TOKEN_REVOKED)
        end
    else Authentication Failure
        Auth0->>User: Error message (invalid credentials)
    end
```

#### 6.4.5.2 Authorization Flow Diagram

```mermaid
graph TB
    Start([Authenticated API Request]) --> ExtractContext[Extract User Context<br/>from JWT Claims]
    ExtractContext --> CheckPermission{Has Required<br/>Permission in JWT?}
    
    CheckPermission -->|No| PermissionDenied[Return 403 Forbidden<br/>INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS]
    CheckPermission -->|Yes| CheckResourceOwnership{Resource<br/>Ownership Check}
    
    CheckResourceOwnership --> QueryDB[Query MongoDB<br/>for Resource]
    QueryDB --> ResourceExists{Resource<br/>Exists?}
    
    ResourceExists -->|No| NotFound[Return 404 Not Found]
    ResourceExists -->|Yes| OwnershipValidation{User Owns Resource<br/>OR is Admin?}
    
    OwnershipValidation -->|No| PermissionDenied
    OwnershipValidation -->|Yes| AuditLog[Log Authorization Decision<br/>to audit_logs collection]
    
    AuditLog --> ExecuteOperation[Execute Business Logic<br/>Process Request]
    ExecuteOperation --> Success[Return 200 OK]
    
    PermissionDenied --> AuditLogDenied[Log Permission Denied Event]
    AuditLogDenied --> End([End])
    
    NotFound --> End
    Success --> End
    
    style CheckPermission fill:#FFE4B5
    style CheckResourceOwnership fill:#FFE4B5

## 6.5 Monitoring and Observability

### 6.5.1 Monitoring Architecture Overview

#### 6.5.1.1 Observability Strategy

The NewNov_6_1 system implements a comprehensive observability architecture built on the **three pillars of observability**—metrics, logs, and distributed traces—providing complete visibility into system health, performance, and user experience. As documented in Section 1.3 (System Overview), the system is currently in initialization phase with no implementation code; all monitoring specifications represent planned architecture awaiting implementation.

**Strategic Monitoring Objectives:**

- **Proactive Issue Detection**: Identify performance degradation and failures before user impact through predictive alerting and anomaly detection
- **Root Cause Analysis**: Enable rapid troubleshooting through correlated metrics, logs, and traces with sub-second query performance
- **Capacity Planning**: Track resource utilization trends to inform scaling decisions and cost optimization
- **SLA Compliance**: Monitor 99.9% availability target and latency SLAs across all service tiers
- **Security Monitoring**: Detect suspicious activities, authentication failures, and security policy violations in real-time
- **Cost Optimization**: Track infrastructure and LLM API costs to identify optimization opportunities

**Observability Maturity Model:**

| Maturity Level | Capabilities | Target Timeline |
|---------------|--------------|-----------------|
| **Level 1: Reactive** | Basic CloudWatch metrics, manual log review | Launch (Month 0) |
| **Level 2: Proactive** | Automated alerting, structured logging, dashboards | Month 3 |
| **Level 3: Predictive** | Anomaly detection, synthetic monitoring, trace analysis | Month 6 |
| **Level 4: AI-Driven** | ML-based alerting, automated remediation, predictive scaling | Year 2 |

#### 6.5.1.2 Monitoring Stack Technology Architecture

**AWS-Native Monitoring Approach:**

The system leverages AWS managed services for monitoring, eliminating operational overhead while providing enterprise-grade observability capabilities:

| Component | Technology | Role | Justification |
|-----------|-----------|------|---------------|
| **Metrics Platform** | AWS CloudWatch Metrics | Time-series metrics collection and storage | Native AWS integration, zero-configuration, 15-month retention |
| **Logging Platform** | AWS CloudWatch Logs | Centralized log aggregation and analysis | Native ECS integration, CloudWatch Logs Insights query engine |
| **Distributed Tracing** | AWS X-Ray (Planned) | Request tracing across services | Native AWS integration, service map visualization |
| **Alerting Engine** | CloudWatch Alarms + SNS | Threshold-based alerting | Real-time notification, integration with PagerDuty/Slack |

**External Monitoring Integrations:**

- **MongoDB Atlas Metrics**: Database-specific metrics (connection pool, query performance, replication lag)
- **Auth0 Logs**: Authentication events, login failures, security anomalies
- **PagerDuty**: Critical alert escalation and on-call management
- **Slack**: Team collaboration and warning-level notifications

### 6.5.2 Metrics Collection

#### 6.5.2.1 Infrastructure Metrics

**AWS Service Metrics (Automatic Collection):**

CloudWatch automatically collects metrics from all AWS infrastructure components without agent installation:

**Application Load Balancer Metrics:**

| Metric Name | Description | Unit | Normal Range |
|------------|-------------|------|--------------|
| `RequestCount` | Total HTTP/HTTPS requests | Count | 100-10,000/min |
| `TargetResponseTime` | Time for target to respond | Seconds | <0.5s P99 |
| `HTTPCode_Target_2XX_Count` | Successful responses | Count | >95% of total |
| `HTTPCode_Target_4XX_Count` | Client errors | Count | <2% of total |

**ECS Container Metrics:**

| Metric Name | Description | Unit | Normal Range |
|------------|-------------|------|--------------|
| `CPUUtilization` | Container CPU usage | Percent | 30-70% average |
| `MemoryUtilization` | Container memory usage | Percent | 40-80% average |
| `NetworkRxBytes` | Network bytes received | Bytes | Variable |
| `NetworkTxBytes` | Network bytes transmitted | Bytes | Variable |

**ElastiCache Redis Metrics:**

| Metric Name | Description | Unit | Alert Threshold |
|------------|-------------|------|-----------------|
| `CacheHitRate` | Percentage of cache hits | Percent | <70% warning |
| `CurrConnections` | Active connections | Count | >90% max warning |
| `DatabaseMemoryUsagePercentage` | Memory utilization | Percent | >85% warning |
| `NetworkBytesIn` | Network traffic in | Bytes/sec | Capacity planning |

### 6.5.3 Log Aggregation and Management

#### 6.5.3.1 Structured Logging Architecture

**JSON Logging Standard:**

All application logs emit structured JSON format enabling machine-parseable log analysis through CloudWatch Logs Insights:

**Standard Log Entry Schema:**

| Field | Type | Required | Description |
|-------|------|----------|-------------|
| `timestamp` | ISO8601 | Yes | UTC timestamp |
| `level` | String | Yes | DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR, CRITICAL |
| `service` | String | Yes | flask-api, celery-worker |
| `environment` | String | Yes | production, staging, development |

**Request Context Fields:**

- `request_id`: Unique correlation ID (UUID) for request tracing
- `user_id`: Authenticated user identifier
- `method`: HTTP method (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE)
- `path`: API endpoint path
- `status_code`: HTTP response status
- `response_time_ms`: Request processing duration
- `ip_address`: Client IP address (anonymized per GDPR)

**Error Context Fields:**

- `error_type`: Exception class name
- `error_message`: Exception message (sensitive data scrubbed)
- `stack_trace`: Full stack trace for debugging
- `affected_resource`: Resource ID that triggered error

#### 6.5.3.2 Log Collection Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant App as Flask Application
    participant Stdout as stdout/stderr
    participant ECS as ECS Log Driver
    participant CWLogs as CloudWatch Logs
    participant S3 as S3 Archive
    participant Glacier as S3 Glacier
    
    App->>Stdout: Write structured JSON log
    Stdout->>ECS: ECS captures container output
    ECS->>CWLogs: Stream logs to CloudWatch Logs
    
    Note over CWLogs: Hot storage (90 days)
    
    CWLogs->>S3: Lifecycle policy after 90 days
    Note over S3: Warm storage (30 days)
    
    S3->>Glacier: Lifecycle policy after 30 days
    Note over Glacier: Cold storage (7 years)
    
    Note over App,Glacier: Automatic log scrubbing:<br/>passwords, tokens, PII redacted
```

#### 6.5.3.3 Log Retention and Archival Policy

**Log Retention by Environment:**

| Environment | CloudWatch Retention | S3 Archive | Glacier Archive | Total Retention |
|-------------|---------------------|------------|-----------------|-----------------|
| **Production** | 90 days | 30 days | 7 years | 7 years total |
| **Staging** | 30 days | 90 days | None | 120 days total |
| **Development** | 7 days | None | None | 7 days total |

**Log Groups Organization:**

```
/aws/ecs/production/flask-api          # Flask API request logs
/aws/ecs/production/celery-worker      # Background job logs
/aws/alb/production                    # Load balancer access logs
/aws/lambda/production/*               # Serverless function logs (if used)
```

**Sensitive Data Scrubbing:**

As documented in Section 5.4.2.3 (Cross-Cutting Concerns), sensitive data is automatically scrubbed from all logs:

- Passwords and authentication credentials → `[PASSWORD_REDACTED]`
- Credit card numbers → `[CC_REDACTED]`
- API keys and secrets → `[API_KEY_REDACTED]`
- Session tokens → `[TOKEN_REDACTED]`
- Email addresses → Partially masked (first 3 chars visible)
